question: Avery attacks with a [Guile] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron], and Nelson blocks with [Jerrard of the Closed Fist]. Does Avery shuffle?
answer:
Short answer: the rules provided here don't settle it, so I can't give you a definitive yes or no.

What I can say from the context:

1. While it's on the battlefield face down (turned face down by Ixidron), Guile has no name, no abilities, and only the characteristics granted by the effect that made it face down — rule [708.2b] says a face-down permanent has no characteristics other than those listed by the ability or rules that allowed it to be face down. So while face down, that permanent does not have Guile's "When Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner's library" ability as a battlefield object.

2. Guile's ability is a "from anywhere" trigger, so the question is whether it triggers based on the Guile card that arrives in the graveyard (where a face-down permanent's face-down status ends). The context does not include the rules on zone changes, on what happens to a face-down permanent's identity as it leaves the battlefield, or on which object's abilities are checked for a "put into a graveyard from anywhere" trigger. That's the missing piece.

3. What the context does confirm is only the downstream behavior: if Guile's ability does trigger, the shuffle happens robustly. Rule [701.24c] uses Guile as its own example — if it's put into a graveyard, the ability triggers, and even if someone exiles the card from the graveyard in response, Avery's library is still shuffled when the ability resolves. Rule [701.24d] and [701.24e] similarly confirm a library gets shuffled even when zero objects actually move or the library is nearly empty.

Also note a factual precondition: nothing in the question establishes that the face-down Guile actually dies. A face-down creature made by Ixidron is a small vanilla creature; whether Jerrard of the Closed Fist deals it lethal damage (and whether Jerrard of the Closed Fist survives) determines whether anything is put into a graveyard at all. If neither creature dies in combat, there is no trigger and no shuffle regardless of the above.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Guile is still face down at the moment combat damage is dealt. If it were turned face up before damage, it would plainly have its own ability on the battlefield and dying would trigger the shuffle. I'm also treating this as a two-player exchange between Avery and Nelson; nothing in the provided rules changes that analysis at a multiplayer table, though the provided context includes only limited multiplayer material ([807.2b] on Grand Melee attack-left), so a multiplayer table's attack requirements could differ.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.400.7: An object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence. This rule has the following exceptions.
gold_text.603.10: Normally, objects that exist immediately after an event are checked to see if the event matched any trigger conditions, and continuous effects that exist at that time are used to determine what the trigger conditions are and what the objects involved in the event look like. However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows:
gold_text.603.6c: Trigger events that involve objects changing zones are called “zone-change triggers.” Many abilities with zone-change triggers attempt to do something to that object after it changes zones. During resolution, these abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to. If the object is unable to be found in the zone it went to, the part of the ability attempting to do something to the object will fail to do anything. The ability could be unable to find the object because the object never entered the specified zone, because it left the zone before the ability resolved, or because it is in a zone that is hidden from a player, such as a library or an opponent’s hand. (This rule applies even if the object leaves the zone and returns again before the ability resolves.) The most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield triggers and leaves-the-battlefield triggers. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent moves from the battlefield to another zone, or when a phased-in permanent leaves the game because its owner leaves the game. These are written as, but aren’t limited to, “When [this object] leaves the battlefield, . . .” or “Whenever [something] is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, . . . .” (See also rule 603.10.) An ability that attempts to do something to the card that left the battlefield checks for it only in the first zone that it went to. An ability that triggers when a card is put into a certain zone “from anywhere” is never treated as a leaves-the-battlefield ability, even if an object is put into that zone from the battlefield.

cited_text.708.2b: Face-down spells and face-down permanents have no characteristics other than those listed by the ability or rules that allowed the spell or permanent to be face down. Any listed characteristics are the copiable values of that object’s characteristics. (See rule 613, “Interaction of Continuous Effects,” and rule 707, “Copying Objects.”) A face-down permanent can’t be turned face down. If a spell or ability attempts to turn a face-down permanent face down, nothing happens and that effect doesn’t change any of its characteristics or their copiable values.
cited_text.701.24c: Shuffle If an effect would cause a player to shuffle one or more specific objects into a library, that library is shuffled even if none of those objects are in the zone they’re expected to be in or an effect causes all of those objects to be moved to another zone or remain in their current zone. Guile says, in part, “When Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner’s library.” It’s put into a graveyard and its ability triggers, then a player exiles it from that graveyard in response. When the ability resolves, the library is shuffled. Black Sun’s Zenith says, in part, “Shuffle Black Sun’s Zenith into its owner’s library.” Black Sun’s Zenith is in a graveyard, has gained flashback (due to Recoup, perhaps), and is cast from that graveyard. Black Sun’s Zenith will be exiled, and its owner’s library will be shuffled.
cited_text.701.24d: Shuffle If an effect would cause a player to shuffle a set of objects into a library, that library is shuffled even if there are no objects in that set. Loaming Shaman says “When this creature enters, target player shuffles any number of target cards from their graveyard into their library.” It enters the battlefield, its ability triggers, and no cards are targeted. When the ability resolves, the targeted player will still have to shuffle their library.
cited_text.701.24e: Shuffle If an effect causes a player to shuffle a library containing zero or one cards, abilities that trigger when a library is shuffled will still trigger.
cited_text.807.2b: Any multiplayer options used are decided before play begins. The Grand Melee variant uses the following default options. The attack left option is used (see rule 803).

answer_gold:
Yes. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. At that point, the Guile is face-up in the graveyard and has that ability.

(Guile's trigger does not fit the exception for "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers because it is a "from anywhere" trigger.)

question: Archer attacks with a [The Scarab God] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron] and Nia blocks with [Scathe Zombies]. Does The Scarab God trigger?
answer:
I can't settle this with the material provided. The provided context includes no oracle text for The Scarab God, Ixidron, or Scathe Zombies, and no rule stating that a face-down permanent is a 2/2 with no name, no creature types, and no abilities — that's the key rule this question hinges on, and it isn't in the context.

What the context does support:
- The only face-down rules given are [708.3] (objects put onto the battlefield face down are turned face down before entering, so enters-the-battlefield abilities don't trigger or apply) and [708.12] (an effect that reveals a face-down permanent uses that object's characteristics ignoring continuous effects). Neither tells us whether a creature turned face down by Ixidron keeps its printed triggered abilities.
- On the combat side, [509.1i] establishes that abilities triggering on blockers being declared trigger when the defending player declares blockers, and [509.3c] covers "becomes blocked" triggers, while [508.1m]/[508.3] cover "attacks" triggers. So if The Scarab God had a relevant combat trigger and did have its abilities, the trigger would go on the stack at the appropriate declaration step.
- [603.2f] also notes an ability doesn't trigger if its object is at no time visible to all players; a face-down permanent on the battlefield is visible as an object, so that rule isn't what stops it.

To answer properly I'd need The Scarab God's actual ability text (and confirmation that it even has a trigger tied to attacking or becoming blocked) plus the rule on characteristics of face-down permanents. Note also that the answer here doesn't depend on player count — the same declare-blockers timing applies with two players or more, though with more than two players the defending player is the one whose player or planeswalker/battle is being attacked.

answer_gold: No. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. However, "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers check the game state immediately before the event instead. At that point, The Scarab God had no abilities.

question: Alaia casts [Biogenic Upgrade] targeting [Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11]. In total how many counters are be placed on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11?
answer:
I can't answer this with what I've been given. The context includes no card data for Biogenic Upgrade and none for Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11, so I don't know how many counters Biogenic Upgrade places, whether it distributes them among one or more targets, or whether Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 has any counter-modifying ability (such as one that adds extra counters or caps the number of counters it can have).

What the provided rules do tell me, in case doubling is involved: to double the number of a kind of counters on a permanent, you give that permanent as many of those counters as it already has [701.10e] — so a permanent with N counters ends up with 2N. Also, if Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 had an ability saying it can't have more than N counters of a kind, all but N would be removed as a state-based action [704.5r] [122.4]. And +1/+1 counters change power and toughness in layer 7c [122.1a] [613.4c].

To give you a number, I'd need the oracle text of Biogenic Upgrade and of Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.1a: Some continuous effects are replacement effects. Like prevention effects (see rule 615), replacement effects apply continuously as events happen—they aren’t locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word “instead” to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.
gold_text.701.10e: Double To double the number of a kind of counters on a player or permanent, give that player or permanent as many of those counters as that player or permanent already has.

cited_text.701.10e: Double To double the number of a kind of counters on a player or permanent, give that player or permanent as many of those counters as that player or permanent already has.
cited_text.704.5r: The state-based actions are as follows: If a permanent with an ability that says it can’t have more than N counters of a certain kind on it has more than N counters of that kind on it, all but N of those counters are removed from it.
cited_text.122.4: If a permanent with an ability that says it can’t have more than N counters of a certain kind on it has more than N counters of that kind on it, all but N of those counters are removed from it as a state-based action. See rule 704.
cited_text.122.1a: A counter is a marker placed on an object or player that modifies its characteristics and/or interacts with a rule, ability, or effect. Counters are not objects and have no characteristics. Notably, a counter is not a token, and a token is not a counter. Counters with the same name or description are interchangeable. A +X/+Y counter on a creature or on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield, where X and Y are numbers, adds X to that object’s power and Y to that object’s toughness. Similarly, -X/-Y counters subtract from power and toughness. See rule 613.4c.
cited_text.613.4c: Within layer 7, apply effects in a series of sublayers in the order described below. Within each sublayer, apply effects in timestamp order. (See rule 613.7.) Note that dependency may alter the order in which effects are applied within a sublayer. (See rule 613.8.) Layer 7c: Effects and counters that modify power and/or toughness (but don’t set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value) are applied.

answer_gold: Nine. Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's ability is a replacement effect that applies whenever counters are being placed on it When Biogenic Upgrade begins resolving, that replacement effect will add a counter, resulting in Alaia placing four +1/+1 counters. Afterwards, Biogenic Upgrade will then double the amount of counters on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11. This results in an additional four counters being placed on it, which will then be modified by Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's replacement effect again, resulting in nine +1/+1 counters in total.

question: Addison casts [Ferocious Zheng]. After it resolves, they cast [Elemental Eruption] and reveal [Everdream] from their hand, splicing it onto Elemental Eruption. When Elemental Eruption's Storm trigger resolves, will the copies of Elemental Eruption also have Everdream spliced onto them?
answer:
Yes. The Storm copies of Elemental Eruption will each have Everdream's rules text on them.

Why: splicing is a keyword ability that lets you reveal a card with splice from your hand and add its rules text to a spell you're casting; the spell then has the characteristics of the main spell plus the rules text of the spliced card, as a text-changing effect [702.47c] [612.10]. So once Everdream is spliced onto Elemental Eruption, the Elemental Eruption on the stack simply *has* that text as part of its characteristics.

Storm reads "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn," and copying a spell copies both its characteristics and all decisions made for it, including targets and modes [702.40a] [707.10]. Since the spliced Everdream text is part of Elemental Eruption's characteristics on the stack, each copy has it too. Note also that text gained by splice which refers to a card by name refers to the spell on the stack — so on each copy, any "Everdream" text acts as Elemental Eruption [702.47c] [201.5b]. Targets for the added text are chosen normally when casting, and you may choose new targets for any of the copies [702.47d] [702.40a].

Count: Ferocious Zheng was cast earlier this turn, so it counts as one "other spell cast before it this turn," giving at least one copy (add one per any other spell cast by any player earlier that turn — this counting is the same in two-player and multiplayer games, since it counts all spells cast that turn, not just yours).

One caveat: the splice text only lasts while that spell is on the stack — Elemental Eruption loses the splice changes once it leaves the stack for any reason [702.47e]. That doesn't affect the copies, which are separate spells on the stack that already have the text.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.601.2b: To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). If the spell is modal, the player announces the mode choice (see rule 700.2). If the player wishes to splice any cards onto the spell (see rule 702.47), they reveal those cards in their hand. If the spell has alternative or additional costs that will be paid as it’s being cast such as buyback or kicker costs (see rules 118.8 and 118.9), the player announces their intentions to pay any or all of those costs (see rule 601.2f). A player can’t apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. If the spell has a variable cost that will be paid as it’s being cast (such as an {X} in its mana cost; see rule 107.3), the player announces the value of that variable. If the value of that variable is defined in the text of the spell by a choice that player would make later in the announcement or resolution of the spell, that player makes that choice at this time instead of that later time. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes hybrid mana symbols, the player announces the nonhybrid equivalent cost they intend to pay. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes Phyrexian mana symbols, the player announces whether they intend to pay 2 life or a corresponding colored mana cost for each of those symbols. Previously made choices (such as choosing to cast a spell with flashback from a graveyard or choosing to cast a creature with morph face down) may restrict the player’s options when making these choices.
gold_text.702.47a: Splice Splice is a static ability that functions while a card is in your hand. “Splice onto [quality] [cost]” means “You may reveal this card from your hand as you cast a [quality] spell. If you do, that spell gains the text of this card’s rules text and you pay [cost] as an additional cost to cast that spell.” Paying a card’s splice cost follows the rules for paying additional costs in rules 601.2b and 601.2f–h. Since the card with splice remains in the player’s hand, it can later be cast normally or spliced onto another spell. It can even be discarded to pay a “discard a card” cost of the spell it’s spliced onto.
gold_text.707.2: When copying an object, the copy acquires the copiable values of the original object’s characteristics and, for an object on the stack, choices made when casting or activating it (mode, targets, the value of X, whether it was kicked, how it will affect multiple targets, and so on). The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object (that text being name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, by its face-down status, and by “as . . . enters” and “as . . . is turned face up” abilities that set power and toughness (and may also set additional characteristics). Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied. Chimeric Staff is an artifact that reads, “{X}: This artifact becomes an X/X Construct artifact creature until end of turn.” Clone is a creature that reads, “You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield.” After a Staff has become a 5/5 Construct artifact creature, a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of it. The Clone is an artifact, not a 5/5 Construct artifact creature. (The copy has the Staff’s ability, however, and will become a creature if that ability is activated.) Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of a face-down Grinning Demon (a creature with morph {2}{B}{B}). The Clone is a colorless 2/2 creature with no name, no types, no abilities, and no mana cost. It will still be face up. Its controller can’t pay {2}{B}{B} to turn it face up.

cited_text.702.47c: Splice The spell has the characteristics of the main spell, plus the rules text of each of the spliced cards. This is a text-changing effect (see rule 612, “Text-Changing Effects”). The spell doesn’t gain any other characteristics (name, mana cost, color, supertypes, card types, subtypes, etc.) of the spliced cards. Text gained by the spell that refers to a card by name refers to the spell on the stack, not the card from which the text was copied. Glacial Ray is a red card with splice onto Arcane that reads, “Glacial Ray deals 2 damage to any target.” Suppose Glacial Ray is spliced onto Reach Through Mists, a blue spell. The spell is still blue, and Reach Through Mists deals the damage. This means that the ability can target a creature with protection from red and deal 2 damage to that creature.
cited_text.702.47d: Splice Choose targets for the added text normally (see rule 601.2c). Note that a spell with one or more targets won’t resolve if all of its targets are illegal on resolution.
cited_text.702.47e: Splice The spell loses any splice changes once it leaves the stack for any reason.
cited_text.702.40a: Storm Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack. “Storm” means “When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn. If the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for any of the copies.”
cited_text.707.10: To copy a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and a copy of an activated ability isn’t activated. A copy of a spell or ability copies both the characteristics of the spell or ability and all decisions made for it, including modes, targets, the value of X, and additional or alternative costs. (See rule 601, “Casting Spells.”) Choices that are normally made on resolution are not copied. If an effect of the copy refers to objects used to pay its costs, it uses the objects used to pay the costs of the original spell or ability. A copy of a spell is owned by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell or ability is controlled by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell is itself a spell, even though it has no spell card associated with it. A copy of an ability is itself an ability. A player casts Fork, targeting an Emerald Charm. Fork reads, “Copy target instant or sorcery spell, except that the copy is red. You may choose new targets for the copy.” Emerald Charm is a modal green instant. When the Fork resolves, it puts a copy of the Emerald Charm on the stack except the copy is red, not green. The copy has the same mode that was chosen for the original Emerald Charm. It does not necessarily have the same target, but only because Fork allows choosing of new targets. Fling is an instant that reads, “As an additional cost to cast this spell, sacrifice a creature” and “Fling deals damage equal to the sacrificed creature’s power to any target.” When determining how much damage a copy of Fling deals, it checks the power of the creature sacrificed to pay for the original Fling. Dawnglow Infusion is a sorcery that reads, “You gain X life if {G} was spent to cast this spell and X life if {W} was spent to cast it.” Because mana isn’t an object, a copy of Dawnglow Infusion won’t cause you to gain any life, no matter what mana was spent to cast the original spell.
cited_text.612.10: A splice ability changes a spell’s text by adding the rules text of the card with splice to the spell, following that spell’s own rules text. It doesn’t modify or replace any of that spell’s own text. (See rule 702.47, “Splice.”)
cited_text.201.5b: Text that refers to the object it’s on by name means just that particular object and not any other objects with that name, regardless of any name changes caused by game effects. If an ability of an object refers to that object by name, and an object with a different name gains that ability, each instance of the first name in the gained ability that refers to the first object by name should be treated as the second name. Quicksilver Elemental says, in part, “{U}: This creature gains all activated abilities of target creature until end of turn.” If it gains an ability that says “{BB}: Regenerate Skithiryx,” activating that ability will regenerate Quicksilver Elemental, not the Skithiryx, the Blight Dragon it gained the ability from. Glacial Ray is an instant with splice onto Arcane that says “Glacial Ray deals 2 damage to any target.” If it’s spliced onto a Kodama’s Reach, that Kodama’s Reach deals 2 damage to the target. The Ever-Changing ’Dane says “{1}, Sacrifice another creature: The Ever-Changing ’Dane becomes a copy of the sacrificed creature, except it has this ability.” Its ability is activated sacrificing a Runeclaw Bear. The Ever-Changing ’Dane becomes a copy of Runeclaw Bear and gains an ability that should be treated as saying “{1}, Sacrifice another creature: Runeclaw Bear becomes a copy of the sacrificed creature, except it has this ability.”

answer_gold: Yes. As Addison is casting Elemental Eruption they choose whether they want to splice as part of the casting process. When the storm trigger resolves it copies all the choices made when casting the original spell, including the choice to splice.

question: Nova controls a [Torsten Von Ursus] enchanted by their [Felidar Umbra]. Allen activates the last ability of [Sorin, Lord of Innistrad], targeting the Torsten Von Ursus. What happens?
answer:
I can't resolve this with what I've been given. The context includes the umbra armor rules and no card data for Torsten Von Ursus, Felidar Umbra, or Sorin, Lord of Innistrad, so I can't say what Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's last ability actually does to Torsten Von Ursus (or even whether that ability targets at all).

What I can state from the provided rules: umbra armor is a static ability found on some Auras, and it means "If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura" [702.89a]. So if Felidar Umbra grants umbra armor and some effect would destroy Torsten Von Ursus, that destruction is replaced: all damage marked on Torsten Von Ursus is removed and Felidar Umbra is destroyed instead. Umbra armor does nothing against effects that exile, sacrifice, return to hand, or reduce toughness to 0 — only against destruction. (Note also that older cards printed with "totem armor" now read umbra armor in Oracle [702.89b].)

To answer the actual question I'd need Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's oracle text for its last ability, plus Felidar Umbra's text confirming it grants umbra armor. Also, whether the ability's effect reaches only one opponent or every opponent could matter at a multiplayer table, but no multiplayer rule was provided here either.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

What an Aura can be attached to is defined by its enchant keyword ability (see rule 702.5, “Enchant”). Other effects can limit what a permanent can be enchanted by. If an Aura is entering the battlefield under a player’s control by any means other than by resolving as an Aura spell, and the effect putting it onto the battlefield doesn’t specify the object or player the Aura will enchant, that player chooses what it will enchant as the Aura enters the battlefield. The player must choose a legal object or player according to the Aura’s enchant ability and any other applicable effects.

answer_gold: The Felidar Umbra is destroyed instead of the Torsten Von Ursus. It is then returned to the battlefield by the rest of Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability. The only creature on the battlefield is the Torsten Von Ursus, so the Felidar Umbra must enter the battlefield enchanting the Torsten Von Ursus. Felidar Umbra is now controlled by Allen.

question: Nico controls [Containment Priest]. Alma attempts to play [Dryad Arbor], which is exiled. Can Alma now play [Sequestered Stash] as their land for turn?
answer:
No — Alma has already played their land for the turn, so they can't play Sequestered Stash (assuming no effect grants additional land drops).

Why: Dryad Arbor is both a land and a creature, and an object that's both a land and another card type can only be played as a land; it can't be cast as a spell [305.9] [300.2a]. So Alma's action was the special action of playing a land — putting it onto the battlefield from hand, using no stack [305.1] [701.18a].

That land drop is spent the moment the special action is taken. To see whether another land can be played, you compare the number of lands Alma may play this turn with the number they've already played this turn; normally that's one and one, so the play isn't legal [305.2a] [305.2b]. Nothing about Dryad Arbor being exiled afterward by Containment Priest's replacement effect "rewinds" the land drop — Dryad Arbor did leave the hand as a played land, and once it changes zones it's a new object with no memory of its prior existence [400.7i]. Even if an effect tried to let Alma play another land, a "can't play a land" restriction would win over a permission [101.2].

Alma could still play Sequestered Stash only if some continuous effect (e.g., an "you may play an additional land this turn" effect) had raised their land limit above one [305.2a].

question: Autumn attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Light Up the Stage] from Nehemiah's library. Can Autumn pay Light Up the Stage's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
answer:
No. Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost is {R} — one red mana — and {C} is colorless mana specifically, which never satisfies a colored mana symbol. Autumn can't pay it with only {C}.

Details:
- Spectacle is a static ability functioning on the stack that says "You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell's mana cost if an opponent lost life this turn" [702.137a]. It's an alternative cost, not a cost reduction, so it replaces the whole {2}{R} mana cost with {R}. Because the spectacle cost itself contains a colored symbol, that symbol must be paid with red mana.
- A player can't pay a cost without the resources to pay it fully, and partial payments aren't allowed [118.3], [601.2h]. One {C} in Autumn's mana pool simply cannot be spent on {R} unless some effect lets Autumn spend mana as though it were mana of any color — and even then, that only changes how the cost may be paid, not the cost itself [609.4b].
- Two separate conditions also have to hold before spectacle is even an option: an opponent must have lost life this turn [702.137a], and Autumn must be legally allowed to cast Light Up the Stage from exile at all (Robber of the Rich grants that permission on its own terms; that text isn't in the provided context, so I'm not ruling on the window or attack-condition here).

Timing note: I'm assuming Autumn is trying to cast Light Up the Stage after some opponent has already lost life this turn. If no opponent has lost life yet at the moment Autumn proposes the spell, spectacle isn't available at all and Autumn would have to pay the full {2}{R} [702.137a].

Multiplayer: the answer is the same with two players or more — spectacle only asks that an opponent (any one of them) lost life this turn [702.137a], and the {R} requirement is unaffected by player count.

question: Autumn controls [Bridge from Below] and [Silvercoat Lion]. They cast [Hour of Revelation]. Do they create a Zombie token?

Immediately before Hour of Revelation destroyed everything, Bridge from Below was still on the battlefield, not in the graveyard, so the graveyard-only ability wasn't there to trigger when Silvercoat Lion died. question: Axl activates [Ring of Ma'rûf]'s ability in their upkeep. What happens in Axl's draw step if they don't own any cards outside the game?
answer:
Short answer: in Axl's draw step the draw is replaced, Axl gets no card (there's nothing outside the game to choose), and Axl does not draw and does not lose the game to an empty library because of this.

Why: the Ring of Ma'rûf effect is a replacement effect that replaces Axl's next card draw with choosing a card they own from outside the game and putting it into their hand. "Outside the game" means anywhere that isn't one of the game's zones — sideboard/personal collection in sanctioned play — and it is not a zone itself [400.11c]. An effect that replaces a card draw still applies even if no card could actually be drawn [121.6a] [614.11], so the turn-based draw at the start of Axl's draw step [504.1] is replaced rather than performed.

Because the replacement lets a player choose an appropriate card they own from outside the game [701.23j], if Axl owns no such cards there is simply nothing to choose and no card enters Axl's hand. Crucially, since the draw event was replaced, Axl never "attempted to draw a card from a library with no cards in it," so the state-based action that makes such a player lose the game [704.5b] [121.4] doesn't apply on account of the replaced draw. (If Axl's library happens to be empty and a later, unreplaced draw is required, that separate draw would cause the loss.)

Assumption on timing: I'm reading it as the ability resolving in the upkeep so the replacement is already in place before the draw step begins; if it somehow resolved after the draw-step draw had already happened, it would instead apply to Axl's next draw after that.

Player count doesn't change any of this — the provided rules here are the same with two players or more than two.

question: Amani controls [Leyline of the Void] and casts [Hypnotic Cloud] to have Nicolas discard a card. Nicolas discards [Loxodon Smiter]. Does it end up on the battlefield or in exile?
answer:
Nicolas chooses, and in practice Loxodon Smiter goes to the battlefield under Nicolas's control.

Why: both effects are replacement effects trying to modify the same event — "Loxodon Smiter is put into Nicolas's graveyard from his hand." Loxodon Smiter's own printed text says that if a spell or ability an opponent controls (here Amani's Hypnotic Cloud) would cause its owner to discard it, it's put onto the battlefield instead of into the graveyard. Amani's Leyline of the Void says a card that would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere is exiled instead. Note that Loxodon Smiter's own text overrides the ordinary discard rule that a discarded card goes to its owner's graveyard ([Discard], [701.9c]).

When two replacement effects would apply to the same event of a card being put into a zone, the affected player chooses which one to apply — the same principle the rules illustrate with Leyline of the Void competing against Wheel of Sun and Moon in [712.21d], where the affected player picks one effect to apply. Here the affected player is Nicolas (the discarding player and the card's owner), not Amani, so Nicolas will normally choose Loxodon Smiter's replacement. Once that applies, Loxodon Smiter enters the battlefield and is never put into a graveyard, so Leyline of the Void's effect has nothing to replace and it is not exiled. It enters under Nicolas's control, since he's the player the effect puts it onto the battlefield for ([110.2a]).

If Nicolas instead chose Leyline of the Void's effect, Loxodon Smiter would be exiled and would not hit the battlefield — but that choice is his, not Amani's.

Multiplayer: nothing changes. The choice belongs to the affected player (Nicolas) regardless of the number of players; Leyline of the Void applies to Amani's opponents, and Loxodon Smiter's clause keys off a spell an opponent of its owner controls.

Caveat: the exact oracle text of Loxodon Smiter, Leyline of the Void's full text, and the general replacement-effect-choice rule (616.1) were not supplied in the context; I relied on the Leyline of the Void wording quoted inside [712.21d] and on the choice principle shown there.

question: In a Commander game with 4 players, Ari casts [Kardur, Doomscourge]. Bode controls [Oxidda Finisher], and [Parhelion II], which is not a creature at the time Kardur, Doomscourge's enter the battlefield ability resolves. During Bode's next turn, can they attack Ari with Parhelion II? Can they have the Angel tokens created by Parhelion II attack Ari?
answer:
The provided context doesn't contain what's needed to answer this fully. Kardur, Doomscourge's oracle text isn't included in the card data, and no rules about goading (the mechanic Kardur, Doomscourge uses, which forces a creature to attack and to attack a player other than the goader if able) appear in the rules excerpts given. Without those, I can't state authoritatively whether Parhelion II or the Angel tokens created by Parhelion II are under any attack requirement or restriction with respect to Ari.

What the provided rules do establish, for a 4-player Commander game: creatures can attack only opponents within their controller's range of influence, planeswalkers those opponents control, and battles those opponents protect [801.3], and only a creature can attack [506.3]. In Commander with 4 players everyone is normally within everyone's range of influence, so absent some other effect, Bode could declare an attack on Ari with any untapped creature Bode controls, announcing which player, planeswalker, or battle each attacker is attacking [508.1b]. Note that Parhelion II can only attack at all if it is a creature (i.e., crewed) at the time attackers are declared, since only creatures can attack [506.3, 302.5]. Optional attack-left/attack-right or Emperor seating restrictions [803.1a, 803.1b, 809.3c, 811.4] would change this, but those aren't used in standard Commander.

To resolve the actual question — whether Kardur, Doomscourge's ability applied to Parhelion II (which was a noncreature Vehicle when the ability resolved) and to the Angel tokens created afterward — I'd need Kardur, Doomscourge's card text and the goad rules.

answer_gold:
Bode cannot attack Ari with Parhelion II, but they can choose for the Angel tokens to attack Ari.

Kardur, Doomscourge's enters-the-battlefield ability sets up a rules change that causes any creatures Ari's opponents control to have to attack if able and to have to attack another player if able. Since this is a change in the rules of the game, it affects Parhelion II even if it is not a creature at the time the ability resolves.

The Angel tokens are created attacking, but are never declared as attackers. Because of this, Bode can choose Ari to be the defending player for the tokens.

question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: assuming Jinx sets Urza's Saga's land type to a basic land type of Alexzander's choice, Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities for as long as that effect lasts, so it is not sacrificed and it stops getting lore counters — it just sits there as a mana-producing land (still an enchantment, still with two lore counters on it).

Why:
- Rule [305.7]: when an effect sets a land's subtype to one or more basic land types, the land loses its old land types and loses all abilities generated from its rules text and old land types, gaining instead the mana ability for the new basic type. Urza's Saga's chapter abilities are printed rules-text abilities (chapter symbols are keyword abilities representing triggered abilities, [107.15a], [714.2b]), so they're gone. It keeps its supertypes and card types ([305.7], [205.4b]) — it's still an enchantment land, and losing the land type doesn't strip the Saga enchantment subtype or the counters already on it.
- The 'sacrifice the Saga' state-based action only applies to "a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities" ([704.5s], [714.4]). With no chapter abilities, Urza's Saga is never sacrificed, even though 2 counters is at/over what its final chapter would have been if it had chapter III (2 is less than 3 anyway, but the point holds if a third counter were somehow added).
- Likewise, the precombat main phase turn-based action puts a lore counter only on each Saga its controller controls "with one or more chapter abilities" ([505.4], [703.4f], [714.3c]). So Nico's Urza's Saga gets no counter on Nico's next precombat main phase while the effect lasts.

When the effect ends (Jinx-style effects are typically 'until end of turn' — I'm assuming that duration since Jinx's text wasn't provided): the chapter abilities come back, Urza's Saga resumes getting lore counters at the start of Nico's precombat main phase, and once its counters reach its final chapter number the sacrifice state-based action applies again ([704.5s]).

Note: if Jinx instead only *adds* a land type rather than setting it, [305.7] says the land keeps its own types and rules text, so Urza's Saga would keep all chapter abilities and behave normally.

Player count doesn't change any of this — the rules cited ([505.4], [703.4f]) work off "the active player" and each Saga's controller, so it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Abel crews their [Adrestia]. Nathalie activates their [Mobilized District] causing it to become a creature. After that resolves, Nathalie casts [Mirrorweave] targeting their Mobilized District. What are Adrestia's characteristics after Mirrorweave resolves?
answer:
Adrestia becomes a copy of Mobilized District as it is printed — i.e., a nonbasic land named Mobilized District with Mobilized District's printed abilities — and it does NOT copy the fact that Mobilized District is currently animated into a creature.

Why: a copy effect operates in layer 1 and copies only the object's copiable values — the values derived from the printed text (name, mana cost, color indicator, card types, subtypes, supertypes, rules text, power, toughness, loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, face-down status, and "as . . . enters" abilities. Other continuous effects, specifically including type-changing effects, plus status and counters, are not copied [707.2, 707.2a, 613.1a, 613.2a]. Nathalie's Mobilized District activation is a type-changing effect (layer 4), so it is not part of Mobilized District's copiable values. This is exactly the Chimeric Staff/Clone example in the rules: after Chimeric Staff has become a 5/5 Construct artifact creature, a Clone copying it is just an artifact with the activated ability, not a 5/5 creature [707.2].

So after Mirrorweave resolves, in layer 1 Adrestia's copiable values become Mobilized District's printed values: name Mobilized District, no mana cost, colorless, card type Land (not a Vehicle, no printed power/toughness), and Mobilized District's printed abilities (including its own animation ability, which Abel could activate later).

Two things that survive on top of that copy, because they apply in later layers and aren't copied: Adrestia's crewed status. Crewing makes the object an artifact creature until end of turn via a type-changing effect that applies after layer 1 [613.1a, 613.2a], so Adrestia is still an artifact creature in addition to being a land named Mobilized District. Note that the crew effect only changes types; it doesn't set power and toughness, and the copied printed values supply none, so Adrestia would have no defined power/toughness from either source (effectively 0/0). Any counters or damage on Adrestia are likewise untouched by the copy [707.2].

Timing note: I'm assuming Mirrorweave resolved after both the crew and the Mobilized District animation had already resolved, as stated. If Mobilized District were animated after Mirrorweave resolved, nothing about Adrestia would change anyway, since Mirrorweave locked in the copiable values at the time it resolved.

Caveat: the exact printed text of Adrestia, Mirrorweave, and Mobilized District wasn't supplied in my context, so I'm answering from the general copy rules; the copy-vs-type-changing conclusion above holds regardless of table size, and nothing here differs between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

question: Ari controls a [Lunarch Inquisitors] that exiled a [Jasmine Boreal] when it transformed. Nyla casts [Moonmist]. Does the Jasmine Boreal return to the battlefield?
answer:
No — Jasmine Boreal stays exiled. Ari's Lunarch Inquisitors exiled Jasmine Boreal "until Lunarch Inquisitors leaves the battlefield." Transforming is not a zone change: a permanent that transforms stays on the battlefield as the same permanent, just with its other face up (rule 712.9 describes transforming as something that happens to a permanent already on the battlefield). Since the specified event (Lunarch Inquisitors leaving the battlefield) hasn't occurred, the second one-shot effect that would return the exiled card is never created, so Jasmine Boreal doesn't come back (rule 610.3c).

Two caveats:
- Moonmist reads "Transform all Humans." Whether Nyla's Moonmist even affects Ari's Lunarch Inquisitors depends on whether that face is a Human, which the provided context doesn't tell us. Either way the answer is the same: transforming it (or not) leaves it on the battlefield, so Jasmine Boreal stays exiled.
- Only permanents represented by double-faced tokens or non-meld double-faced cards can transform at all (rule 712.9); if Lunarch Inquisitors weren't such a permanent, nothing would happen.

Jasmine Boreal returns only if Lunarch Inquisitors actually leaves the battlefield (dies, is exiled, bounced, etc.); at that point the return effect applies (rule 610.3c), and the card returns under its owner's control unless stated otherwise. If instead Ari's Lunarch Inquisitors left the game entirely because Ari left a multiplayer game, note that a triggered ability controlled by a player who has left the game isn't put on the stack (rule 800.4d), which can strand the exiled card; in a two-player game that scenario ends the game instead.

Ironfang will continue to get +2/+2 until end of turn.

question: Addison controls [Carth the Lion] and [Bioessence Hydra]. Addison activates the [+1] ability of [Dovin, Architect of Law]. How many times does Bioessence Hydra trigger?
answer:
Once — assuming Bioessence Hydra's ability triggers on loyalty counters being put on a planeswalker you control, that happens as a single event here, not two.

Why: Carth the Lion makes loyalty abilities of planeswalkers you control cost an additional [+1] to activate. Rule 606.5 says that when the total cost to activate a loyalty ability contains multiple costs to add or remove loyalty counters, those costs are combined into a single cost to add or remove loyalty counters. So activating the [+1] ability of Dovin, Architect of Law with Carth the Lion out is not "+1 then +1"; it is one combined cost of putting two loyalty counters on Dovin, Architect of Law at the same time. One event, so one trigger — and if Bioessence Hydra's ability counts how many loyalty counters were put on, it counts two.

Caveat you should know: Bioessence Hydra's oracle text was not provided to me, so I'm answering the structural question (how many separate counter-placement events occur), which is one. If Bioessence Hydra instead triggered on something like "whenever a loyalty ability is activated," that would still be a single activation and thus a single trigger.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only Addison's own permanents are involved.

question: Amani has 3 life. Briar casts [Chain of Plasma], targeting Amani. As it resolves, Amani pays the cost to copy it, and chooses to have the copy target Campbell. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: Amani takes 2 damage from Briar's Chain of Plasma (dropping from 3 life to 1), and then a copy of Chain of Plasma is put onto the stack under Amani's control, targeting Campbell. That copy is a separate spell on the stack; it resolves before Briar's original has finished? No — Briar's original has already finished resolving at that point, so the copy is the next thing to resolve, dealing 2 damage to Campbell, and Campbell then gets the same discard-and-copy option in turn.

Details and the rules behind it:
- The copy Amani creates is controlled and owned by Amani, because a copy of a spell is controlled by the player under whose control it was put onto the stack, and a copy of a spell is itself a spell even though there's no card for it [707.10]. It was not "cast," so cast-triggers don't fire [707.10].
- The copy duplicates all decisions made for the original (modes, X, additional costs), but since Chain of Plasma's copy effect lets its controller choose new targets, Amani may legally redirect it to Campbell; only the final set of targets is checked for legality [707.10c], [115.7e]. A new target must be a legal target [707.10c].
- Because Amani controls the copy, Amani is the one whose spell deals the 2 damage to Campbell, which matters for effects that care about who dealt the damage.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the standard sequence for Chain of Plasma — the damage is dealt to Amani first, then Amani discards and creates the copy, all during the resolution of Briar's spell. If instead the copy were somehow made before the damage, Amani would still end at 1 life; only the relative order of the two damage events would change.

Multiplayer note: this is a three-or-more-player game (Amani, Briar, Campbell), and nothing here changes for that — each copy simply has a single new target chosen by that copy's controller. If a limited range of influence ("range of influence") variant is in use, a player choosing a target must choose one within their own range of influence [801.5a].

One caveat: Chain of Plasma's own card text was not provided in my context, so the specific numbers (2 damage, discard a card as the cost to copy) are from the question's premise; the copy mechanics above are grounded in the provided rules. question: In a multiplayer game, Achilles uses [Jon Irenicus, Shattered One] to give [Vastwood Gorger] to Brynn. If Brynn dies, what happens to Vastwood Gorger?
answer:
Vastwood Gorger is exiled (assuming Achilles owns it and Brynn merely controls it via Jon Irenicus, Shattered One).

Details: when a player "dies" in a multiplayer game, they leave the game. At that moment, first all objects owned by the departing player leave the game with them, and any effects giving that player control of objects or players end; then any objects on the stack they controlled that aren't cards cease to exist; then any objects still controlled by that player are exiled [800.4a]. The control-change from Jon Irenicus, Shattered One has no duration, so it isn't an "effect giving Brynn control" that simply ends and reverts — Vastwood Gorger is still controlled by Brynn as they leave, so it is exiled. This is not a state-based action; it happens immediately when Brynn leaves [800.4a].

Two variations:
- If Brynn is actually the owner of Vastwood Gorger (for example Achilles had earlier taken it and then handed it over), then it leaves the game entirely along with Brynn rather than being exiled [800.4a].
- If instead the control effect were temporary and it ended while Brynn was already gone, Vastwood Gorger would be exiled at that moment under [800.4c] rather than reverting to a player who is no longer in the game.

This whole question is multiplayer-specific: in a two-player game, one player leaving simply ends the game, so nothing needs to happen to Vastwood Gorger.

Note: Jon Irenicus, Shattered One's own card text wasn't provided here; if its ability has a duration or a built-in clause about the creature, that printed text would override the general expectation of a permanent control change.

question: Aspen attacks with [Hammers of Moradin]. During the combat damage step, they use [Time Stop] to end the turn. What happens to the tokens created by myriad?
answer:
Short answer: the myriad tokens stay on the battlefield — Time Stop skips the end of combat step, so the delayed "exile the tokens at end of combat" ability never triggers.

Details:

1. Myriad on Hammers of Moradin reads "Whenever this creature attacks, for each opponent other than defending player, you may create a token that's a copy of this creature that's tapped and attacking that player or a planeswalker they control. If one or more tokens are created this way, exile the tokens at end of combat" [702.116a]. The exile clause is a delayed triggered ability that triggers at the beginning of the end of combat step [511.2].

2. Time Stop ends the turn. When an effect ends the turn, the current phase/step ends immediately, all creatures and planeswalkers are removed from combat, and the game skips straight to the cleanup step, skipping every phase and step in between — including the end of combat step [724.1d]. Because that step is skipped, the delayed "at end of combat" trigger simply never triggers (compare the parallel wording for end-of-combat triggers being skipped in [724.2e] and for end step triggers in [724.1e]).

3. Any abilities that had already triggered before Time Stop resolved but hadn't yet been put on the stack cease to exist [724.1a]. No player gets priority during the process, and any abilities that trigger during it go on the stack in the cleanup step [724.1f]. In the cleanup step, damage is removed and "until end of turn"/"this turn" effects end [514.2], [703.4p] — none of which destroys or exiles the tokens.

So the myriad copies of Hammers of Moradin remain on the battlefield indefinitely, no longer attacking (they were removed from combat).

Multiplayer note: myriad only creates tokens when there are opponents other than the defending player, so this scenario inherently assumes a multiplayer game; in a two-player game no myriad tokens would have been created at all. The provided rules don't include anything about tokens ceasing to exist as a state-based action, so this answer is grounded only in the skipped end-of-combat trigger.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Time Stop resolved after the myriad tokens were already created (during the combat damage step, as stated). If Time Stop had somehow resolved while the myriad trigger itself was still waiting to be put on the stack, that trigger would cease to exist [724.1a] and no tokens would ever be created.

question: If Avery is going first, they'd like to reveal [Umori, the Collector] as their companion. If they're going second, they don't want to have a companion. Can they do this?
answer:
Yes. Revealing a companion happens *after* the starting player has been determined, so Avery already knows whether they're going first before deciding whether to reveal Umori, the Collector.

Rule 103.2b puts the companion reveal among the additional pre-game steps performed after the starting player is determined, and rule 702.139a likewise says the reveal happens "before the game begins" as part of that 103.2b procedure. So Avery may look at who won the die roll / who is the starting player, then choose to reveal Umori, the Collector only if they are going first, and reveal nothing if they aren't. Revealing is always optional ("you may reveal"), and no more than one card may be revealed this way, only if the deck fulfills the companion condition (with "starting deck" meaning the deck after sideboard cards are set aside, and in Commander before the commander is set aside — 702.139b).

Practical notes: the revealed Umori, the Collector stays outside the game; later, once during the game, any time Avery has priority with an empty stack during a main phase of their turn, they may pay {3} (three generic mana) as a special action that doesn't use the stack to put it into their hand (702.139a, 116.2g), after which it remains in the game (702.139c).

This works the same at a two-player table and in multiplayer: in a multiplayer game the starting player is likewise determined first, so Avery can condition the reveal on whether they are the starting player (103.2b). Note that in multiplayer, "going second" isn't the only alternative — they simply reveal nothing if they aren't first.

question: Ada controls [Ethersworn Canonist]. They want to suspend [Shade of Trokair] and then cast [Divination]. Can they?
answer:
Yes — assuming Ethersworn Canonist reads "Each player who has cast a spell this turn can't cast additional nonartifact spells," and that Ada hasn't cast anything yet this turn, Ada can suspend Shade of Trokair and then still cast Divination.

Why:

1. Suspending is a special action, not casting. A player with a suspend card in hand may exile it with time counters; this action doesn't use the stack [116.2f], [702.62a]. Because it isn't casting a spell, it doesn't make Ethersworn Canonist's "has cast a spell this turn" condition true.

2. But the special action has a gate: Ada may take it only if they could begin to cast Shade of Trokair by putting it onto the stack from hand [116.2f], [702.62a], and effects that would prohibit casting that card are taken into account [702.62c], [601.3]. Since Ada hasn't cast a spell yet this turn, Ethersworn Canonist isn't prohibiting anything, so the gate is satisfied. (Shade of Trokair is a sorcery-speed permanent card, so the suspend action must be taken at a time Ada could begin casting it — their own main phase, empty stack, with priority [117.1a].)

3. Casting Divination afterward is then the first spell Ada has cast this turn, so Ethersworn Canonist doesn't stop it [601.3].

Order matters: if Ada had already cast a nonartifact spell this turn, Ethersworn Canonist would prohibit casting Shade of Trokair, and therefore Ada could not even take the suspend special action [702.62c], [116.2f]. Likewise, if Ada casts Divination first, they can no longer suspend Shade of Trokair that turn.

Also note that when the last time counter is later removed, the resulting triggered ability lets Ada play Shade of Trokair — that is casting, and Ethersworn Canonist could prohibit it at that time [702.62a].

Two caveats: (a) I'm relying on the commonly known text of Ethersworn Canonist, Shade of Trokair, and Divination — none of their card text was supplied in my context, so verify the wording. (b) Nothing here changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game; Ethersworn Canonist's restriction is applied per player.

question: Natasha and Nico are playing Two-Headed Giant, and each controls their own copy of [Bloodbond Vampire]. Ariel controls [Wall of Shards], and on their next upkeep they put the third age counter on it. Can Ariel have Natasha gain one life and Nico gain two? If so, how many triggered abilities of Bloodbond Vampire will be put on the stack?
answer:
Yes, Ariel can split it: Natasha gains 1 life and Nico gains 2 life, and two Bloodbond Vampire triggers go on the stack (one for Natasha's Bloodbond Vampire, one for Nico's Bloodbond Vampire).

Why the split is legal: with three age counters, the cumulative upkeep cost is paid three times over, and each instance of "an opponent gains 1 life" lets Ariel choose an opponent independently, so Ariel may pick Natasha once and Nico twice. Cumulative upkeep counts the age counters on the permanent when the ability resolves, and the payment scales with them (see [702.24b] for how age counters and repeated cumulative upkeep payments work).

Why it's two triggers, not three: in Two-Headed Giant, damage, life loss, and life gain happen to each player individually, and only the result is applied to the team's shared life total ([810.9], [Shared Life Total]). So Natasha's 1 life gained is Natasha's life-gain event and Nico's 2 life gained is Nico's life-gain event; Natasha's team's shared life total goes up by 3 total. Bloodbond Vampire reads "Whenever you gain life" — that means its own controller. Natasha's Bloodbond Vampire sees only Natasha's gain, and Nico's Bloodbond Vampire sees only Nico's gain. Nico's 2 life comes from one simultaneous payment, so it's a single life-gain event for Nico, not two. (Compare [702.15e], where separate simultaneous sources produce separate life-gain events and thus multiple triggers.)

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Ariel makes all three choices as part of paying the single cumulative upkeep cost on this upkeep, so the life gains happen simultaneously. If instead Nico's two points arrived as two distinct life-gain events at different times, Nico's Bloodbond Vampire would trigger twice, for three triggers total.

Caveat: this whole answer is framed for the Two-Headed Giant variant, which is inherently multiplayer; the shared-life-total rules I cite are specific to that variant. In an ordinary two-player game there would be no shared life total and no teammate to split the life gain between. Note also that Two-Headed Giant can be played with larger equal teams ([810.11]), where the same per-player life-gain rule applies.

One gap: the exact text of Wall of Shards wasn't provided in the context, so I'm relying on the standard cumulative upkeep framework in [702.24b] for how the repeated payments work.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

Then you may pay [cost] for each age counter on it. If you don’t, sacrifice it.” If [cost] has choices associated with it, each choice is made separately for each age counter, then either the entire set of costs is paid, or none of them is paid. Partial payments aren’t allowed. A creature has “Cumulative upkeep {W} or {U}” and two age counters on it. When its ability next triggers and resolves, the creature’s controller puts an age counter on it and then may pay {W}{W}{W}, {W}{W}{U}, {W}{U}{U}, or {U}{U}{U} to keep the creature on the battlefield. A creature has “Cumulative upkeep—Sacrifice a creature” and one age counter on it. When its ability next triggers and resolves, its controller can’t choose the same creature to sacrifice twice. Either two different creatures must be sacrificed, or the creature with cumulative upkeep must be sacrificed.

answer_gold: Paying Wall of Shards' cumulative upkeep involves the choice of an opponent. The choice for each age counter is made individually, then the whole cost is paid at once. This means Ariel can make the stated choice, and the result of this is Natasha gains one life and Nico gains two life. Because of this, each player's Bloodbond Vampire will trigger separately, causing two instances of the triggered ability to be put on the stack. Although the players share a life total, gaining life happens to each player individually.

question: Nataly controls [Urza's Saga] with 2 lore counters on it. Alex casts [Magus of the Moon]. What does Urza's Saga look like?
answer:
Direct answer: Urza's Saga becomes a Mountain land with no abilities — it keeps its 2 lore counters, but because it no longer has any chapter abilities, it is not sacrificed and it stops advancing.

Caveat on grounding: the context I was given does not include the oracle text of Urza's Saga or Magus of the Moon, so I'm working from the standard assumption that Magus of the Moon makes each nonbasic land (including the land-Saga Urza's Saga) a Mountain with no other card types, subtypes, or abilities. Take the type/ability-stripping part as that assumption, not as something the provided rules establish.

Given that assumption, the Saga rules give clear results:
- Nataly's precombat main phase turn-based action only puts a lore counter on each Saga she controls that has one or more chapter abilities [505.4] [703.4f] [714.3c]. With its chapter abilities gone, Urza's Saga gets no new lore counter.
- The sacrifice state-based action likewise only applies to a Saga permanent "with one or more chapter abilities" whose lore counters equal or exceed its final chapter number [704.5s] [714.4]. With no chapter abilities (and arguably no Saga subtype at all), Urza's Saga is not sacrificed, even though 2 counters would otherwise be close to or at its final chapter.
- The 2 lore counters physically remain on the permanent; nothing removes them. Chapter abilities are triggered abilities represented by chapter symbols [107.15] [714.2b], so with those abilities stripped, nothing can trigger from counters being added later either.

If Magus of the Moon later leaves the battlefield, Urza's Saga regains its chapter abilities with 2 lore counters still on it, and the sacrifice state-based action [704.5s] is then checked again immediately.

Player count: nothing here depends on the number of players — the lore-counter turn-based action is per active player [505.4], so it works the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Niko controls [Metallurgeon] and [Ornithopter of Paradise]. Avery casts [Prismari Command], choosing the "deal 2 damage" and "destroy target artifact" modes, targeting Ornithopter of Paradise with both. In response, Niko activates Metallurgeon's ability targeting Ornithopter of Paradise. What happens?
answer:
I can't fully answer this from the provided material. The context doesn't include the oracle text of Metallurgeon or Prismari Command, and it contains no rules about shield counters (the counter Metallurgeon's ability is normally associated with), nor the rule about modal spells resolving their chosen modes in the order printed. Without those, I can't say authoritatively how many of Prismari Command's two effects on Ornithopter of Paradise get absorbed.

What the provided rules do tell you, in case it helps frame the interaction:

- A replacement effect that applies to Ornithopter of Paradise being destroyed replaces that destruction event; regeneration is the classic example of this (701.8c).
- If two or more replacement or prevention effects would apply to the same event affecting Ornithopter of Paradise, Niko (as its controller) picks one to apply, then the process repeats with whatever is still applicable (616.1e, 616.1f). That choice rule is per event, though \effevents - damage and destruction - are separate events, so a single one-shot replacement does not automatically cover both.
- Nothing here says a shield counter is even a replacement effect, so I won't assert how it interacts.

To resolve this properly I'd need: Metallurgeon's exact activated-ability text, Prismari Command's exact text and mode-ordering, and the rules on shield counters (rule 122/704-area text) plus the modal-spell rule.

This discussion is not affected by player count; nothing above depends on whether there are two players or more.

question: Asa controls an [Inventors' Fair], a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], and two [Piston Sledge]. They want to activate the last ability of Inventors' Fair and sacrifice a Piston Sledge to help pay the cost. Is this legal?
answer:

question: Ashley controls [Tatterkite]. Ashley casts [Genesis Wave], putting [Phylactery Lich] and [Humility] onto the battlefield. Can they put a phylactery counter on Tatterkite?
answer:
Yes — assuming Humility is on the battlefield alongside Tatterkite at the time, Ashley can put the phylactery counter on Tatterkite.

Why: Tatterkite's relevant ability is the one saying counters can't be put on it. That kind of ability is unusual in that it functions as the object enters the battlefield as well as while it's on the battlefield [113.6i], and normally a "can't" effect beats a permission to place counters [101.2a].

But Humility removes abilities from all creatures. Ability-removing effects are applied in layer 6 of the continuous-effect layer system [613.1f], and once Humility's effect applies, Tatterkite simply no longer has the "counters can't be put on it" ability at all. Note the distinction: Humility takes the ability away, it doesn't say Tatterkite "can't have" that ability, so this isn't the harder case in [113.11] where an ability can never be re-added — and losing an ability is genuinely ability removal rather than a stated quality of the object [113.12]. With no such ability, there's no "can't" effect left to override the counter placement [101.2a].

Timing assumption: Genesis Wave puts Phylactery Lich and Humility onto the battlefield simultaneously, so Humility is already applying when Phylactery Lich's as-enters counter-placement choice is made — hence the counter can go on Tatterkite (assuming Tatterkite otherwise qualifies as the artifact Phylactery Lich requires). If instead Humility somehow arrived after Phylactery Lich had already entered, the choice would have been made while Tatterkite still had its ability, and the counter could not have been placed there then.

Player count doesn't matter here: the interaction is entirely between Ashley's own permanents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Caveat: the exact oracle text of Tatterkite, Humility, Phylactery Lich, and Genesis Wave wasn't supplied in the context, so this answer relies on their commonly stated effects as described in your question.

question: Aubrey and Arely are playing 2HG. Aubrey attacks with [Coral Commando] and Arely casts [Flash Conscription] to gain control of Coral Commando after it's been declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step. Is it still attacking?
answer:
No — Coral Commando is removed from combat and stops being an attacking creature.

Rule 506.4a lists the ways a permanent is removed from combat, and one of them is that its controller changes. When Flash Conscription resolves and Arely gains control of Coral Commando, that control change removes Coral Commando from combat; a creature removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature. It won't deal combat damage in the combat damage step, and nothing will be blocking it.

This is true even though Aubrey and Arely are on the same team in Two-Headed Giant. Rule 805.10b tells us that under the shared team turns option the active team declares attackers as a group and announces what each attacking creature is attacking, but it doesn't make teammates a single controller — control of Coral Commando genuinely changes from Aubrey to Arely, so 506.4a applies. (If they were on opposing teams, the same answer holds for the same reason.)

Two related points: Coral Commando was still legally declared as an attacker, so any abilities that already triggered on attackers being declared (rule 508.3) still resolve normally, and Aubrey is still considered to have "attacked" that defending player for effects that check that (rule 508.6). Also, rule 506.4a's last sentence — that effects which would have kept a creature from attacking don't remove it from combat once declared — doesn't help here, because Flash Conscription isn't such an effect; it's a control-change effect, which is expressly listed as removing the permanent from combat.

I'm assuming Flash Conscription resolved during the declare attackers step after attackers were declared, as stated. If instead it had resolved before attackers were declared, Coral Commando simply would never have been declared as an attacker by Aubrey.

question: Alonso controls [Spark Double] and casts [Clone]. Clone enters the battlefield with exactly one +1/+1 counter, no matter how many times Alonso reapplies the copy effect.

Why: Spark Double's copy ability is a replacement effect with an "except it enters with a +1/+1 counter on it" clause. That clause is an additional effect, not a modification of the copy's copiable characteristics. Rule 707.9e states that if another copy effect is applied to that object after applying the copy effect that carried the exception, the exception's effect doesn't happen — this is exactly the Altered Ego/Clone example given in that rule.

So as Alonso chains the applications: the first time Clone copies Spark Double, its exception would grant a counter, but because Alonso then applies the copy effect Clone inherited (copying Spark Double again), that earlier exception is wiped out. The same happens for the second and third applications. Only the fourth and final application of the copy effect — the one after which no further copy effect is applied — actually delivers its exception, giving one +1/+1 counter.

Note also that each copy application is part of the single event of Clone entering the battlefield; rule 614.13b's principle that these entry-modifying replacement effects are resolved as Clone enters (and rule 613.2a, layer 1a, where copy effects are applied) means Clone is on the battlefield as a copy of Spark Double with one counter, not with four.

Two points that matter here:

1. Choosing zero targets doesn't make an ability unresponsive. A spell or ability that "requires targets" may allow zero targets to be chosen; it is then simply not a targeted ability, but it still exists on the stack normally [115.6]. Objects and players that the ability merely affects without targeting aren't chosen until it resolves [115.10], so nothing about skipping a target choice removes the window to respond.

2. The only common exception is a mana ability: an activated mana ability doesn't use the stack at all, so it can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to — it resolves immediately [605.3b]. An ability that does other things in addition to producing mana (deal damage, make players sacrifice, draw cards, etc.) is not a mana ability, so it does go on the stack and is respondable.

Caveat on grounding: the oracle text of Priest of Forgotten Gods was not provided to me, so I can't verify from the given context whether its ability has any targets at all or whether it qualifies as a mana ability. If its ability only produced mana, it would resolve immediately with no chance to respond [605.3b]; in any other case Nickolas gets priority and may respond.

Multiplayer: the provided rules here are not two-player-specific on this point — every player, in turn order after the ability is put on the stack, gets a chance to respond, so with more than two players other opponents may also respond before the ability resolves. Note also that if the ability affects "each opponent" without targeting them, those players are determined on resolution [115.10], not when it's activated.

question: Antoine owns an [Eternal Scourge] that was exiled by Nico's [Ixalan's Binding]. Can Antoine cast it?
answer:
Short answer: No — Antoine can't cast it, provided Nico's Ixalan's Binding is still on the battlefield.

The governing rule is 601.3/601.3f: a player can begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows that player to cast it AND no rule or effect prohibits that player from casting it. Both halves must be satisfied.

- Eternal Scourge's own permission ("you may cast this card from exile if an opponent exiled it") supplies the "allows" half.
- Ixalan's Binding supplies a prohibition: while it's on the battlefield, its controller's opponents can't cast spells with the same name as the exiled card. Antoine is an opponent of Nico, so that prohibition applies to him, and a prohibition always beats a permission under 601.3.

Note that this is grounded on the printed text of Eternal Scourge and Ixalan's Binding, which was not supplied in my context — I'm relying on the general permission-vs-prohibition rule, so if either card's actual wording differs from the above, re-check it. The exiled Eternal Scourge is a new object in the exile zone (400.7h), but the effect that exiled it can still track it.

If Ixalan's Binding later leaves the battlefield, its prohibition ends; Eternal Scourge remains exiled (Ixalan's Binding doesn't return it), and its own "cast from exile" permission would then let Antoine cast it, since nothing prohibits him anymore.

Multiplayer: this works the same at any table size. Ixalan's Binding restricts each of its controller's opponents, so any player other than Nico who owns an Eternal Scourge exiled by it is likewise locked out; Nico, not being their own opponent, is not restricted (though Nico isn't the owner here and would need separate permission to cast it).

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
Direct answer: with the manifested (face-down) card placed on top, the merged permanent's copiable characteristics come from that face-down top component — a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no mana cost, and no card types beyond creature — while, by the mutate rules given, it has the abilities of every component, i.e. Trumpeting Gnarr's abilities as well.

Why: mutate means "you may pay [mutate cost] instead of the mana cost; the spell becomes a mutating creature spell and targets a non-Human creature with the same owner" [702.140a]. A face-down manifested creature has no creature types, so it isn't Human and is a legal target (assuming Avery owns both). On resolution the Trumpeting Gnarr spell doesn't enter the battlefield; it merges with the target and the controller chooses top or bottom [702.140c], [608.3d], [730.2a]. A merged permanent has only the characteristics of its topmost component [730.2a], and rule 702.140e adds that a mutated permanent "has all abilities of each card and token that represents it. Its other characteristics are derived from the topmost card or token." So: power/toughness 2/2, colorless, nameless, no mana cost (from the face-down top card), plus Trumpeting Gnarr's abilities from the bottom component.

Also, any "whenever this creature mutates" ability — including Trumpeting Gnarr's own — triggers on the merge [702.140d], and effects that referred to the Trumpeting Gnarr spell now refer to the mutated permanent [702.140f]. The characteristic change from merging is a copiable effect applied in layer 1a [613.2a].

Two caveats I must flag honestly: (1) the provided context contains no manifest / face-down permanent rules, so I'm relying on the description of face-down objects appearing in the copy example [707.3] (a face-down creature is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, types, or abilities) for the top component's characteristics; the specific rules governing turning such a merged permanent face up, and whether a face-down permanent's ability-stripping interacts with 702.140e, are not in the context. (2) This analysis is player-count neutral — nothing here depends on the number of opponents, so it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.
