question: Aryana has taken control of an [Ahn-Crop Crasher] from Noe with [Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded], which Aryana exerts. After Aryana ends their turn, will it untap during Noe's untap step?
answer:
No — Ahn-Crop Crasher will not untap during Noe's next untap step; it stays tapped, and the exert effect expires during that step.

Why:

- To exert a permanent means you choose to have it not untap during your next untap step [701.43a]. The "you" here is the player whose ability it is.
- Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded's control effect only changes control of the *player*, not of that player's objects: while Aryana controls Noe, "all objects are controlled by their normal controllers," and Noe is still the active player on Noe's turn [723.3, 723.1]. So Ahn-Crop Crasher remains Noe's permanent, and its exert choice — even though Aryana is the one making Noe's decisions — belongs to Noe. "Your next untap step" therefore means Noe's next untap step.
- During that untap step, the active player (Noe) determines which permanents they control untap and untaps them all simultaneously as a turn-based action; effects can keep one or more permanents from untapping, and Ahn-Crop Crasher is exactly such a permanent [502.3, 703.4c]. No player gets priority in the untap step, so nobody can respond [502.4].
- The exert effect is used up in that step. If Aryana exerted Ahn-Crop Crasher more than once before Noe's untap step, each such effect expires during that same untap step [701.43b], so it still untaps normally on the following turn.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Aryana exerted Ahn-Crop Crasher while controlling Noe during Noe's own turn (attacking with it), so "next untap step" is the untap step of Noe's following turn. If instead Ahn-Crop Crasher had somehow been exerted on a turn other than Noe's, the skipped untap would still be Noe's next untap step — the answer is the same.

Player count: nothing here depends on the number of players; with more than two players the same reasoning applies, and the untap step in question is simply whichever turn Noe next takes [723.1].

Then they untap them all simultaneously. See rule 502.3.

answer_gold: Yes. A player exerting a permanent only causes it to not untap during that player's next untap step, not any untap step that would untap it.

question: Aminah has no cards in their library and activate [Words of Wind] in their upkeep. Do they lose the game?
answer:
No — Aminah doesn't lose the game, provided the replacement effect is in place before the draw would happen and it fully replaces that draw.

Why: a player only loses for an empty library if they actually *attempt to draw* from a library with no cards in it. That's a state-based action, checked the next time a player would receive priority [121.4] [704.5b]. An effect that replaces a card draw is applied even if there were no cards to draw [121.6a]. Since the replacement effect (each player returning a permanent to hand instead of you drawing) applies in place of the draw, no draw attempt ever occurs, so the empty-library state-based action never triggers.

Assumptions and timing: Words of Wind's text wasn't provided in my context, so I'm answering the general principle for a "the next time you would draw a card this turn, [do something] instead" replacement. Ability activated in the upkeep step, so it is in place before the draw step's turn-based draw — that draw gets replaced and Aminah survives. If instead the shield were used up on some earlier draw, or the ability weren't active when Aminah's draw-step draw happened, Aminah would attempt to draw from an empty library and would lose the game the next time a player would receive priority [121.4]. Also note that if an effect merely moves cards from library to hand without the word "draw," that's not a draw at all [121.5], and an impossible instruction does only as much as possible [609.3].

question: After both players finish taking mulligans, Adrian is going second and has both [Gemstone Caverns] and [Chancellor of the Annex] in their hand. Can they reveal Chancellor of the Annex for its ability and also exile it to begin the game with Gemstone Caverns on the battlefield?
answer:
Yes — Adrian can do both, as long as they reveal Chancellor of the Annex first and then exile it to the Gemstone Caverns action.

How it works: both cards work through the "actions from your opening hand" step. Once the mulligan process is finished, the starting player takes any such actions in any order, and then each other player in turn order does the same [103.6]. Since Adrian is not the starting player, Adrian's window comes after the starting player's, and within that window Adrian may take their own opening-hand actions in any order they choose [103.6]. If a card lets a player begin the game with it on the battlefield, that player puts it onto the battlefield during this step [103.6a]; if a card lets a player reveal it from their opening hand, the player does so, and the card remains revealed until the first turn begins, with each card revealable this way only once [103.6b].

Because Adrian chooses the order, they can:
1. Reveal Chancellor of the Annex from the opening hand. Revealing does not move the card out of the hand [701.20b], so Chancellor of the Annex is still in Adrian's hand afterward.
2. Then take Gemstone Caverns' action, putting Gemstone Caverns onto the battlefield and exiling the now-revealed Chancellor of the Annex from hand as the cost of doing so.

The reveal action has already been completed and cannot be taken back or "undone" by the card later leaving the hand; the only limit stated is that each card may be revealed this way only once [103.6b]. If Adrian did it in the reverse order — exiling Chancellor of the Annex to Gemstone Caverns first — Chancellor of the Annex would no longer be in the opening hand and could not be revealed for its ability at all.

Timing caveat: I'm assuming both are done in Adrian's single opening-hand window after the starting player's window, which is how 103.6 structures it; there is no later opportunity to reveal Chancellor of the Annex once the first turn begins.

Assumption about card text: the exact printed text of Gemstone Caverns and Chancellor of the Annex was not supplied in the context, so I'm relying on the general opening-hand-action rules. If either card's own wording restricts the ordering, that printed text would override the general rules.

Multiplayer: the same answer applies with more than two players. Each non-starting player takes their opening-hand actions in turn order after the starting player [103.6], so Adrian still gets a window in which they can order their two actions freely. (In the Two-Headed Giant variant, the starting team's players act first in any order the team likes, then each other team in turn order [805.3b].)

question: Aspen controls [Cosima, God of the Voyage] and mutates [Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt] onto it, putting it underneath Cosima, God of the Voyage. At the beginning of their next upkeep, Aspen exiles Cosima, God of the Voyage to its own triggered ability. What happens?
answer:
Exiling the merged permanent moves one permanent off the battlefield, but both physical cards — Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt — end up in exile as separate cards, and because Aspen is the player exiling the merged permanent, Aspen chooses the relative timestamp order of Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt in exile [730.3b].

Details:
- While merged, the permanent had all abilities of both Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt, with its other characteristics (name, types, P/T, etc.) taken from the top card, Cosima, God of the Voyage [702.140e]. That's why Cosima, God of the Voyage's upkeep ability was available to Aspen at all, and it's why the object being exiled is the whole merged permanent rather than just one card.
- Merging means the mutating spell didn't enter the battlefield separately; Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt became one object with Cosima, God of the Voyage [702.140c].
- When that merged permanent leaves the battlefield, each component card goes to the appropriate zone — here, exile [730.3b, 730.3c]. They are no longer merged; they are two independent cards in exile.
- Because Cosima, God of the Voyage's ability tracks the object it exiled, and an effect that can find the new object(s) a merged permanent becomes as it leaves the battlefield finds all of them and takes the same action on each, when the ability later returns the exiled card to the battlefield it returns both Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt — each as its own separate permanent, not re-merged [730.3c].

Timing note: I'm assuming Aspen chose to exile during the resolution of the beginning-of-upkeep trigger, which is the only point the choice is offered; nothing here depends on any other ordering.

Player count: nothing in this interaction depends on the number of players, so it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table. The rules provided don't include any multiplayer-specific exception for merged permanents.

One gap: the provided context doesn't include Cosima, God of the Voyage's or Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt's own card text, so I can't confirm the exact wording of the counter-accumulating/return clause; the zone-change and "finds all of them" results above are grounded in the merge rules.

question: Aspen controls [Parallel Lives] and a [Caldera Hellion]. They cast [Rite of Replication] targeting the Caldera Hellion. Can Aspen apply the devour replacement effect before the Parallel Lives replacement effect, sacrificing 1 creature to have each token enter with a +1/+1 counter?
answer:
No. Aspen must apply Parallel Lives first, and then apply each token's devour ability separately.

Why: entering the battlefield is an event contained within the event of creating a token, so under rule [616.1g] the replacement effect that changes how many tokens are created (Parallel Lives) has to be chosen before any replacement effect that modifies how those tokens enter the battlefield (Caldera Hellion's devour). Rule [701.7b] likewise separates a replacement effect applying to a token being created from one applying to a token entering the battlefield. So the doubling happens first, and only then does Aspen make the devour choices for each token as it enters.

Devour (here, devour 1) means "as this permanent enters, you may sacrifice any number of creatures; it enters with N +1/+1 counters for each creature sacrificed this way" (see [702.82c] for the devour-[quality] wording of the same template). Because the devour choices are made per token, a single sacrificed creature cannot be counted for more than one token: rule [614.13b] states the same object can't be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how one or more permanents enter the battlefield. So sacrificing one creature gives exactly one token a +1/+1 counter, not all of them.

Also relevant: the devour choices are made before the tokens enter the battlefield ([614.12a]), and since multiple permanents with choice-requiring replacement effects are entering at once, Aspen may not make choices whose combined costs can't be paid — i.e., can't promise the same creature to two tokens ([614.12b]).

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only Aspen's own permanents and choices are involved.

question: Aubrey controls [Exotic Orchard]. Nikolas controls [Crumbling Vestige]. If Aubrey taps Exotic Orchard, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Short answer: I can't give a definitive type without Crumbling Vestige's oracle text, which wasn't provided in the context. Here is exactly how the question resolves once that text is known.

Exotic Orchard's ability is "{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce" (quoted in rule 106.7). So the only thing that matters is what colors of mana the lands Nikolas (and any other opponent of Aubrey) controls "could produce."

- "Could produce" is defined in rule 106.7: it includes any type of mana that an ability of that permanent would produce if that ability were to resolve at that time, taking applicable replacement effects into account in any possible order, and ignoring whether the ability's costs could actually be paid.
- Crucially, Exotic Orchard says "any color." Colorless mana ({C}) is not a color. If the only mana Crumbling Vestige could produce is {C}, then no color is defined, Exotic Orchard's ability produces no mana at all (rule 106.5: an ability that would produce mana of an undefined type produces none instead \u2014 the same outcome rule 106.7 describes when an opponent controls no relevant lands).
- If Crumbling Vestige has an ability that could produce mana of one or more colors, Exotic Orchard could produce any of those colors, and Aubrey chooses one on resolution.

Multiplayer note: rule 106.7's wording is "a land an opponent controls," so in a game with more than two players Aubrey checks the lands of every opponent, not just Nikolas \u2014 any color any of those lands could produce is available. With exactly two players, only Nikolas's lands matter.

What's missing: Crumbling Vestige's printed abilities (in particular whether it has a mana ability that yields a color, such as an enters-the-battlefield mana trigger, versus only a {T}: Add {C} ability). Supply that text and the answer follows mechanically from the bullets above.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

Ignore whether any costs of the ability could or could not be paid. If that permanent wouldn’t produce any mana under these conditions, or no type of mana can be defined this way, there’s no type of mana it could produce. Exotic Orchard has the ability “{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce.” If your opponent controls no lands, activating Exotic Orchard’s mana ability will produce no mana. The same is true if you and your opponent each control no lands other than Exotic Orchards. However, if you control a Forest and an Exotic Orchard, and your opponent controls an Exotic Orchard, then each Exotic Orchard could produce {G}.

question: Azariah, Beckham, and Caelan are playing a multiplayer game. Beckham controls [Stalking Leonin]. Azariah casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Beckham's next turn. After Beckham begins their turn, can Azariah see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
answer:
Yes. While Azariah controls Beckham's turn, rule 723.4 says that any information about an object in the game that would be visible to the player being controlled (Beckham) is also visible to the player controlling them (Azariah). The player chosen for Stalking Leonin is information about a permanent on the battlefield that Beckham knows, so Azariah gets to see it too, along with Beckham's hand and the faces of any face-down creatures Beckham controls.

Some details worth noting:
- The exception in 723.4 is information about cards *outside* the game (e.g., a sideboard/wish board); that stays visible only to Beckham, not to Azariah.
- Only control of the player changes, not control of permanents: Stalking Leonin is still Beckham's permanent, and Beckham is still the active player on their own turn (723.3). Azariah makes the choices and decisions Beckham would make during that turn, including what to play and choices called for by spells and abilities (723.5b), but Beckham still makes their own personal decisions and any choices Beckham is called on to make as themselves (723.8).
- This is a multiplayer game, but the answer is the same as it would be in a two-player game: 723.4 is about the controlled player and the controlling player only. Caelan gains no extra information from Azariah's control of Beckham; Caelan sees only what they would normally see.

One limitation: the text of Stalking Leonin wasn't provided in the context, so I'm answering generally about hidden/known information rather than about any specific secret-choice mechanic that card might use. If Stalking Leonin's chosen player were somehow recorded as information hidden even from Beckham, the provided rules wouldn't grant Azariah access to it either.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

If information about cards outside the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it’s visible only to that player, not the controller of the player. The controller of a player can see that player’s hand and the face of any face-down creatures they control.
cited_text.723.3: Only control of the player changes. All objects are controlled by their normal controllers. A player who’s being controlled during their turn is still the active player.
cited_text.723.5b: While controlling another player, a player makes all choices and decisions the controlled player is allowed to make or is told to make by the rules or by any objects. This includes choices and decisions about what to play, and choices and decisions called for by spells and abilities. The controller of another player can’t make choices or decisions for that player that aren’t called for by the rules or by any objects. The controller also can’t make any choices or decisions for the player that would be called for by the tournament rules. The player who’s being controlled still decides if they will leave to visit the restroom, trade a card to someone else, agree to an intentional draw, or call a judge about an error or infraction.
cited_text.723.8: A player who controls another player also continues to make their own choices and decisions.

answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Beckham. Azariah can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.

question: Angela controls [Mirror Gallery] and two [Sakashima the Impostor]s. One is a copy of their [Master of the Hunt]; the other is copying a wolf token created by Master of the Hunt. They attack with all four creatures. What are the possible bands that Angela may declare?
answer:
I can't answer this one from what I was given. The provided rules cover how bands are declared in general, but the answer depends entirely on the exact printed text of Mirror Gallery, Sakashima the Impostor, and Master of the Hunt (and the Wolf tokens Master of the Hunt makes) — specifically which of those objects actually have banding or a "bands with other [quality]" ability, what the [quality] is, and what names/types the copies end up with. None of that card text or the associated rulings appear in the context above, so any band list I produced would be guesswork.

What the provided rules do establish, and what you'd apply once the card text is known:
- Bands are declared by the active player as attackers are declared; the declaration doesn't use the stack [508.1e], [702.22c].
- A legal band is either (a) one or more attacking creatures with banding plus at most one attacking creature without banding, or (b) one or more attacking creatures with "bands with other [quality]" that themselves have that [quality], together with any number of other attacking creatures that have that [quality] [702.22c].
- Angela may declare as many bands as she likes, but each attacking creature can be in only one band [702.22c].
- Every creature in a band must be attacking the same player, planeswalker, or battle [702.22d], [802.3b].
- Duplicate copies of banding, or of the same kind of "bands with other," on one creature are redundant and don't let it join extra bands [702.22m].
- Once announced, a band lasts the rest of combat even if banding is later removed [702.22e], the creatures remain separate permanents that don't share abilities [702.22g], and if any member becomes blocked, the whole band becomes blocked by that blocker [702.22h], [702.22i].

If you supply the oracle text of Mirror Gallery, Sakashima the Impostor, and Master of the Hunt (including the Wolf token's abilities), I can enumerate the legal bands precisely.

question: Avery controls a Germ token that's equipped with [Barbed Bloodletter]. Nadia controls two [Teferi's Curse]s, one on the Germ, the other on the Barbed Bloodletter. During Avery's untap step, which permanents will phase out? Which of these will phase back in?
answer:
All four permanents phase out: the Germ token, Barbed Bloodletter, and both of Nadia's Teferi's Curses.

Why: phasing is a static ability that modifies the untap step — during Avery's untap step, before untapping, every phased-in permanent with phasing that Avery controls phases out simultaneously ([702.26a], [502.1], [703.4a]). Because each Teferi's Curse grants phasing to the permanent it enchants, both the Germ token and Barbed Bloodletter have phasing and both phase out "directly." Any Aura, Equipment, or Fortification attached to a phasing-out permanent phases out with it, which is called phasing out "indirectly" ([702.26g]) — so the Teferi's Curse on the Germ token and the Teferi's Curse on Barbed Bloodletter both phase out indirectly, even though Nadia controls them. (Barbed Bloodletter would also have gone indirectly with the Germ token, but it phases out directly anyway since it has phasing of its own.) The Germ token keeps existing on the battlefield while phased out rather than ceasing to exist ([702.26d]).

Assuming nothing of Avery's was already phased out, nothing phases in during this untap step (the phase-in half of the turn-based action only brings back permanents that had phased out under Avery's control). They come back during Avery's *next* untap step, when the same turn-based action phases in all permanents that phased out under Avery's control ([702.26a], [502.1]): the Germ token and Barbed Bloodletter phase in directly, and each Teferi's Curse, having phased out indirectly, doesn't phase in on its own but returns along with the permanent it's attached to ([702.26g]). Barbed Bloodletter, which phased out directly, phases in still attached to the Germ token since that object is still on the battlefield ([702.26i]). No attach/unattach or zone-change triggers fire from any of this ([702.26d], [702.26j]).

Two caveats: if an effect makes Avery skip their untap step, the phasing event simply doesn't happen that turn ([702.26m]); and if any effect had instead phased something out "until" a specified event, that permanent wouldn't return via the untap-step action ([610.4a]). This is all independent of player count, though in a multiplayer game, if the controller of a phased-out permanent leaves the game, special rules apply ([702.26n]).

question: It is currently day and Adonis controls [Lazotep Convert] (the back face of [Invasion of Amonkhet]), which is a copy of [Kessig Naturalist]. What happens if it becomes night?
answer:
Nothing happens — Adonis's Lazotep Convert stays as it is, back face up as a copy of Kessig Naturalist.

Why: Kessig Naturalist has daybound, and daybound is three static abilities: "If it is night and this permanent is represented by a double-faced card, it enters transformed," "As it becomes night, if this permanent is front face up, transform it," and "This permanent can't transform except due to its daybound ability" [702.145b]. The transform trigger only applies to a permanent that is *front* face up. Lazotep Convert is the back face of Invasion of Amonkhet, so the permanent is back face up, and the daybound transform clause simply doesn't apply to it. The parallel nightbound rules ([702.145e], [702.145f]) don't help either, because the copy has daybound, not nightbound.

Also note the third clause of daybound: because it can't transform except due to its daybound ability, no other effect can flip Lazotep Convert either. And even if something did try to turn it to its front face, that front face is a battle (Invasion of Amonkhet), not the Kessig Naturalist face — the copy effect only changes its copiable values, not which physical face is up.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming "it becomes night" happens via the normal untap-step day/night check (it's day and the previous turn's active player cast no spells) [502.2], [731.2], [731.2a]. The answer is the same if some other effect makes it night mid-turn [731.1] — the trigger condition (front face up) still isn't met.

Player count doesn't matter here: the day/night check itself can differ in multiplayer games using shared team turns ([731.2a], [731.2b]), but once it's night, Lazotep Convert behaves identically with two players or more.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object (that text being name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, by its face-down status, and by “as . . . enters” and “as . . . is turned face up” abilities that set power and toughness (and may also set additional characteristics). Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied. The Clone is an artifact, not a 5/5 Construct artifact creature. (The copy has the Staff’s ability, however, and will become a creature if that ability is activated.) cited_text.502.2: Second, if it’s day and the previous turn’s active player didn’t cast any spells during that turn, it becomes night. If it’s night and the previous turn’s active player cast two or more spells during that turn, it becomes day. If it’s neither day nor night, this check doesn’t happen and it remains neither. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack. See rule 731, “Day and Night.”
cited_text.731.1: Day and night are designations that the game itself can have. The game starts with neither designation. “It becomes day” and “it becomes night” refer to the game gaining the day or night designation. It can become day or night through the daybound and nightbound keyword abilities (see rule 702.145). Other effects can also make it day or night. Once it has become day or night, the game will have exactly one of those designations from that point forward.

answer_gold: Lazotep Convert will be a copy of Kessig Naturalist. As it becomes night, it will not transform and remain a copy of Kessig Naturalist. Lazotep Convert will only copy the front face of Kessig Naturalist and does not copy its status. When it becomes night, it will not transform because a daybound permanent will only transform as it becomes night if it is front face up. ([702.145b])

question: Adelina's [Fireblade Charger] dies, and Nasir responds with [Thwart the Enemy]. Is the damage prevented?
answer:
I can't answer this one from what's provided. The cards named in the question — "Adelina's Fireblade Charger," "Nasir," and "Thwart the Enemy" — are not in the card data I was given (the only cards provided are Kardur, Doomscourge; Oxidda Finisher; and Parhelion II), so I don't know what damage the trigger would deal or what Thwart the Enemy actually does.

What I can tell you is the general framework that would decide it, in case it helps you check yourself:

- A prevention effect is a "shield" that watches for a damage event and stops some or all of the damage from being dealt; effects using the word "prevent" are prevention effects [615.1a], [Prevent].
- Timing is the usual sticking point: a prevention effect must already exist before the damage event happens. It can't go back in time. Responding to a triggered ability that's still on the stack works; once that ability has resolved and the damage has been dealt, it's too late [615.4].
- If the shield only prevents damage "from a source" with certain properties, the source's properties are rechecked when the damage would be dealt. If they no longer match, nothing is prevented and the shield isn't used up [609.7b], [615.9].
- If the damage is fully prevented, it never happens, and abilities that trigger on damage being dealt don't trigger [615.6], [603.2g].
- If the damage "can't be prevented," the prevention effect is still applied but prevents nothing; any extra effects it has (such as gaining life) still happen, and the shield isn't used up [615.12], [615.12a].
- If the prevention effect has a rider that references the amount prevented, that rider happens immediately after the moment the damage would have occurred [615.5].

Assuming Thwart the Enemy is cast while the death trigger is still on the stack (before it resolves), the timing is legal; if it's cast after that trigger already resolved and dealt damage, nothing is prevented [615.4]. To settle this, I'd need the oracle text of the two cards. Note also that these prevention rules apply the same in two-player and multiplayer games — the provided rules aren't limited to a two-player framing.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.113.7a: The source of an ability is the object that generated it. The source of an activated ability on the stack is the object whose ability was activated. The source of a triggered ability (other than a delayed triggered ability) on the stack, or one that has triggered and is waiting to be put on the stack, is the object whose ability triggered. To determine the source of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7d–f. Once activated or triggered, an ability exists on the stack independently of its source. Destruction or removal of the source after that time won’t affect the ability. Note that some abilities cause a source to do something (for example, “This creature deals 1 damage to any target”) rather than the ability doing anything directly. In these cases, any activated or triggered ability that references information about the source for use while announcing an activated ability or putting a triggered ability on the stack checks that information when the ability is put onto the stack. Otherwise, it will check that information when it resolves. In both instances, if the source is no longer in the zone it’s expected to be in at that time, its last known information is used. The source can still perform the action even though it no longer exists.

cited_text.615.1a: Some continuous effects are prevention effects. Like replacement effects (see rule 614), prevention effects apply continuously as events happen—they aren’t locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a damage event that would happen and completely or partially prevent the damage that would be dealt. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “prevent” are prevention effects. Prevention effects use “prevent” to indicate what damage will not be dealt.
cited_text.Prevent: Prevent. A word used by prevention effects to indicate what damage will not be dealt. See rule 615, “Prevention Effects.”
cited_text.615.4: Prevention effects must exist before the appropriate damage event occurs—they can’t “go back in time” and change something that’s already happened. Spells or abilities that generate these effects are often cast or activated in response to whatever would produce the event and thus resolve before that event would occur. A player can activate an ability that prevents damage in response to a spell that would deal damage. Once the spell resolves, though, it’s too late to prevent the damage.
cited_text.609.7b: Some effects apply to damage from a source—for example, “The next time a red source of your choice would deal damage to you this turn, prevent that damage.” Some effects from resolved spells and abilities prevent or replace damage from sources with certain properties, such as a creature or a source of a particular color. When the source would deal damage, the “shield” rechecks the source’s properties. If the properties no longer match, the damage isn’t prevented or replaced. If for any reason the shield prevents no damage or replaces no damage, the shield isn’t used up.
cited_text.615.9: Some effects generated by the resolution of a spell or ability prevent damage from a source of a player’s choice with certain properties. When the source would deal damage, the shield rechecks the source’s properties. If the properties no longer match, the damage isn’t prevented or replaced and the shield isn’t used up. See rule 609.7b.
cited_text.615.6: If damage that would be dealt is prevented, it never happens. A modified event may occur instead, which may in turn trigger abilities. Note that the modified event may contain instructions that can’t be carried out, in which case the impossible instruction is simply ignored.
cited_text.603.2g: Whenever a game event or game state matches a triggered ability’s trigger event, that ability automatically triggers. The ability doesn’t do anything at this point. An ability triggers only if its trigger event actually occurs. An event that’s prevented or replaced won’t trigger anything. An ability that triggers on damage being dealt won’t trigger if all the damage is prevented.
cited_text.615.12: Some effects state that damage “can’t be prevented.” If unpreventable damage would be dealt, any applicable prevention effects are still applied to it. Those effects won’t prevent any damage, but any additional effects they have will take place. Existing damage prevention shields won’t be reduced by damage that can’t be prevented.
cited_text.615.12a: Some effects state that damage “can’t be prevented.” If unpreventable damage would be dealt, any applicable prevention effects are still applied to it. Those effects won’t prevent any damage, but any additional effects they have will take place. Existing damage prevention shields won’t be reduced by damage that can’t be prevented. A prevention effect is applied to any particular unpreventable damage event just once. It won’t invoke itself repeatedly trying to prevent that damage.
cited_text.615.5: Some prevention effects also include an additional effect, which may refer to the amount of damage that was prevented. The prevention takes place at the time the original event would have happened; the rest of the effect takes place immediately afterward.

answer_gold: Unclear. Fireblade Charger is not currently a creature on the battlefield, but the game uses its last known information to determine how the damage is dealt. If Fireblade Charger only applies to objects that are creatures, like how Biomantic Mastery only counts creatures that actually exist on the battlefield, it won't be prevented. But if Fireblade Charger checks the source of damage to see whether it's a creature, it will be able to identify the damage as coming from a creature. The intention is probably the latter, but Wizards has not clarified.

question: Aminah casts a [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Aminah chooses to put a [Haru-Onna] onto the battlefield and Nico chooses to put a [Domestication] onto the battlefield enchanting Haru-Onna. Who controls the enters-the-battlefield ability of Haru-Onna?
answer:
Nico controls Haru-Onna's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability.

Why: Show and Tell puts both permanents onto the battlefield at the same time. By default Haru-Onna would enter under Aminah's control, since an object put onto the battlefield by an effect enters under the control of the player the effect instructed [110.2a]. But Domestication enters already attached to Haru-Onna (an Aura enters the battlefield attached to the object it will enchant, and the Aura's controller and the enchanted creature's controller need not be the same) [303.4e], and Domestication's static control-changing effect is applied in layer 2 of the characteristic/effect-application order immediately and continuously [613.1b]. So there is no point after they enter at which Aminah controls Haru-Onna — Nico controls it as soon as it's on the battlefield.

A triggered ability that has triggered but is waiting to go on the stack is controlled by the player who controlled its source at the time it triggered [109.4b], and the same is true once it's put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [603.3a][113.8]. Since Nico controlled Haru-Onna at that moment, Nico controls the triggered ability, puts it on the stack, and makes any choices it calls for (and is the "you" of the ability).

Timing note: this assumes Domestication truly enters attached simultaneously with Haru-Onna, which is how Show and Tell's simultaneous puts work. If instead Domestication somehow became attached later (e.g., a separate Aura cast afterward), Haru-Onna's ability would have already triggered while Aminah controlled it, and Aminah would control that trigger.

This reasoning doesn't depend on the number of players: with two players or with more, the trigger's controller is simply whoever controls Haru-Onna at the moment it enters — here, Nico via Domestication.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.303.4f: Some enchantments have the subtype “Aura.” An Aura enters the battlefield attached to an object or player. What an Aura can be attached to is defined by its enchant keyword ability (see rule 702.5, “Enchant”). Other effects can limit what a permanent can be enchanted by. If an Aura is entering the battlefield under a player’s control by any means other than by resolving as an Aura spell, and the effect putting it onto the battlefield doesn’t specify the object or player the Aura will enchant, that player chooses what it will enchant as the Aura enters the battlefield. The player must choose a legal object or player according to the Aura’s enchant ability and any other applicable effects.

cited_text.110.2a: A permanent’s owner is the same as the owner of the card that represents it (unless it’s a token; see rule 111.2). A permanent’s controller is, by default, the player under whose control it entered the battlefield. Every permanent has a controller. If an effect instructs a player to put an object onto the battlefield, that object enters the battlefield under that player’s control unless the effect states otherwise.
cited_text.303.4e: Some enchantments have the subtype “Aura.” An Aura enters the battlefield attached to an object or player. What an Aura can be attached to is defined by its enchant keyword ability (see rule 702.5, “Enchant”). Other effects can limit what a permanent can be enchanted by. An Aura’s controller is separate from the enchanted object’s controller or the enchanted player; the two need not be the same. If an Aura enchants an object, changing control of the object doesn’t change control of the Aura, and vice versa. Only the Aura’s controller can activate its abilities. However, if the Aura grants an ability to the enchanted object (with “gains” or “has”), the enchanted object’s controller is the only one who can activate that ability.
cited_text.613.1b: The values of an object’s characteristics are determined by starting with the actual object. For a card, that means the values of the characteristics printed on that card. For a token or a copy of a spell or card, that means the values of the characteristics defined by the effect that created it. Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order: Layer 2: Control-changing effects are applied.
cited_text.109.4b: Only objects on the stack or on the battlefield have a controller. Objects that are neither on the stack nor on the battlefield aren’t controlled by any player. See rule 108.4. There are six exceptions to this rule: A triggered ability that has triggered but is waiting to be placed on the stack is controlled by the player who controlled its source at the time it triggered, unless it’s a delayed triggered ability. To determine the controller of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7d–f. See also rule 603, “Handling Triggered Abilities.”
cited_text.603.3a: Once an ability has triggered, its controller puts it on the stack as an object that’s not a card the next time a player would receive priority. See rule 117, “Timing and Priority.” The ability becomes the topmost object on the stack. It has the text of the ability that created it, and no other characteristics. It remains on the stack until it’s countered, it resolves, a rule causes it to be removed from the stack, or an effect moves it elsewhere. A triggered ability is controlled by the player who controlled its source at the time it triggered, unless it’s a delayed triggered ability. To determine the controller of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7d–f.
cited_text.113.8: The controller of an activated ability on the stack is the player who activated it. The controller of a triggered ability on the stack (other than a delayed triggered ability) is the player who controlled the ability’s source when it triggered, or, if it had no controller, the player who owned the ability’s source when it triggered. To determine the controller of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7d–f.

answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Nico must choose a permanent that is already on the battlefield for the Domestication to enchant. They can't choose a permanent that is entering at the same time.

question:
Amani controls a [Founding the Third Path], and its third ability is resolving. Amani chooses to cast a [Fatal Push] from their graveyard. Amani currently does not have Revolt.
Can Amani choose to target [Skyhunter Patrol] with Fatal Push? Will Skyhunter Patrol be destroyed by Fatal Push?
answer:
I can't confirm this one from the material provided. The context includes only rules text plus card data for Hammers of Moradin and Time Stop — neither Fatal Push nor Skyhunter Patrol nor Founding the Third Path is included, so I don't have grounded text for Fatal Push's targeting restriction ("mana value 2 or less," raised by revolt) or for Skyhunter Patrol's mana value, and I won't supply those from memory.

What the provided rules do establish, and what will decide the case once you check the two cards' actual text:

- A target must be legal both when the spell is cast and again when it resolves. If a spell's targeting requirement (such as a restriction on the target creature's mana value) isn't met, that object simply can't be chosen as a target at all [115.2]. If it is chosen legally and then stops meeting the requirement, the target is illegal on resolution, and since Fatal Push would have only that one instance of the word "target," the spell wouldn't resolve and would be put into its owner's graveyard [608.2b].
- Whether Amani has revolt is checked as Fatal Push resolves for the destruction effect, but the targeting restriction printed in the targeting clause governs what may be chosen when Fatal Push is cast — so if Skyhunter Patrol's mana value exceeds Fatal Push's non-revolt limit at the time of casting, Skyhunter Patrol simply isn't a legal choice and no targeting is possible [115.2], [608.2b].

Timing note: I'm assuming Amani has no revolt both when Fatal Push is cast and when it resolves. If a permanent left the battlefield under Amani's control in between, revolt could be active on resolution even though it wasn't at cast time — that would change whether a legally chosen target is destroyed, but it would not retroactively make an illegal target choice legal.

This analysis is zone- and player-neutral, so it reads the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; the provided rules include nothing that changes it based on player count. To finish the ruling, supply Fatal Push's oracle text and Skyhunter Patrol's mana cost/mana value.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.714.4: If the number of lore counters on a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities is greater than or equal to its final chapter number, and it isn’t the source of a chapter ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, that Saga’s controller sacrifices it. This state-based action doesn’t use the stack.

cited_text.115.2: Only permanents are legal targets for spells and abilities, unless a spell or ability (a) specifies that it can target an object in another zone or a player, or (b) targets an object that can’t exist on the battlefield, such as a spell or ability. See also rule 115.4.
cited_text.608.2b: If the object that’s resolving is an instant spell, a sorcery spell, or an ability, its resolution may involve several steps. The steps described in rules 608.2a and 608.2b are followed first. The steps described in rules 608.2c–m are then followed as appropriate, in no specific order. The steps described in rule 608.2n and 608.2p are followed last. If the spell or ability specifies targets, it checks whether the targets are still legal. A target that’s no longer in the zone it was in when it was targeted is illegal. Other changes to the game state may cause a target to no longer be legal; for example, its characteristics may have changed or an effect may have changed the text of the spell. If the source of an ability has left the zone it was in, its last known information is used during this process. If all its targets, for every instance of the word “target,” are now illegal, the spell or ability doesn’t resolve. It’s removed from the stack and, if it’s a spell, put into its owner’s graveyard. Otherwise, the spell or ability will resolve normally. Illegal targets, if any, won’t be affected by parts of a resolving spell’s effect for which they’re illegal. Other parts of the effect for which those targets are not illegal may still affect them. If the spell or ability creates any continuous effects that affect game rules (see rule 613.11), those effects don’t apply to illegal targets. If part of the effect requires information about an illegal target, it fails to determine any such information. Any part of the effect that requires that information won’t happen. Sorin’s Thirst is a black instant that reads, “Sorin’s Thirst deals 2 damage to target creature and you gain 2 life.” If the creature isn’t a legal target during the resolution of Sorin’s Thirst (say, if the creature has gained protection from black or left the battlefield), then Sorin’s Thirst doesn’t resolve. Its controller doesn’t gain any life. Plague Spores reads, “Destroy target nonblack creature and target land. They can’t be regenerated.” Suppose the same creature land is chosen both as the nonblack creature and as the land, and the color of the creature land is changed to black before Plague Spores resolves. Plague Spores still resolves because the black creature land is still a legal target for the “target land” part of the spell. The “destroy target nonblack creature” part of the spell won’t affect that permanent, but the “destroy target land” part of the spell will still destroy it. It can’t be regenerated.

answer_gold:
Yes Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol, and it will be destroyed by Fatal Push.

Fatal Push does not check for the target's mana value when put on the stack, so Amani is allowed to target Skyhunter Patrol.

Amani will put Fatal Push on the stack as part of the resolution of Founding the Third Path's third chapter. Once the ability is done resolving, SBAs are checked and the saga is sacrificed. In particular this means that Amani will have Revolt when Fatal Push resolves, thus Skyhunter Patrol will get destroyed.

question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
answer:
Analia ends up controlling both. Analia controls Corrupted Conscience (via Lay Claim), and because Corrupted Conscience gives control of the enchanted creature to Corrupted Conscience's controller, Analia also controls Bane Alley Blackguard.

Why: an Aura's controller is tracked separately from the controller of what it enchants, and changing control of one doesn't change control of the other by itself [303.4e]. Lay Claim enchants Corrupted Conscience and makes Analia its controller. Corrupted Conscience's own control-change effect reads "you control enchanted creature," and "you" means whoever currently controls Corrupted Conscience, so once Analia controls it the Blackguard follows.

Both are control-changing effects applied in layer 2 [613.1b]. Corrupted Conscience's effect depends on Lay Claim's effect (Lay Claim changes who "you" is), so Lay Claim is applied first and Corrupted Conscience's result is recalculated with Analia as its controller. Note Nico never becomes owner of anything here — Analia still owns Bane Alley Blackguard, Nico still owns Corrupted Conscience [110.2b].

One caveat: the exact oracle text of Lay Claim and Corrupted Conscience wasn't provided in my context, so I'm relying on their control-granting wording as described in the question; the rules cited govern the interaction as stated.

Also, Nico losing control of Bane Alley Blackguard is the kind of event that "looks back in time" for leave-control triggers [603.10d]. In multiplayer, if a player later leaves the game, any control effects they created end and their objects leave — e.g., if Analia left, Lay Claim would leave with her and Corrupted Conscience would revert to Nico, giving Nico the creature back again [800.4a]. question: Asher casts [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Asher wants to put [Hall of Triumph] onto the battlefield. Do they know what Noa is putting onto the battlefield while making the choice for Hall of Triumph's replacement effect?
answer:
Yes — by the time Asher makes the color choice for Hall of Triumph's "as this enters" replacement effect, all players have already chosen which cards they're putting onto the battlefield, so Asher can see Noa's card.

Why: Show and Tell has every player choose a card and put it onto the battlefield simultaneously. Those choices are made in APNAP order under rule 101.4b — the active player chooses first, then each other player in turn order, and a player knows the choices previously made. So the two selections happen before anything enters. The permanents then enter the battlefield, and as they move there each other player who will be able to look at them does so, and replacement effects are applied at that point (rule 400.6). Hall of Triumph's "as this enters, choose a color" is a replacement effect that modifies how the permanent enters, and its required choice is made before the permanent enters (rule 614.12a). That choice therefore comes after both cards are known.

What Asher may NOT know: if two or more entering permanents each require a choice from different players at the same time, those choices are also made in APNAP order (rules 616.1f, 101.4b). So if Noa's permanent also has an "as this enters, choose" effect, Asher (if Asher is the active player) makes the Hall of Triumph color choice first, without knowing what Noa will pick; if Noa is the active player, Noa chooses first and Asher gets that information.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading this as the normal case where all Show and Tell selections are made during its resolution before any permanent enters. If instead you imagine the cards entering one at a time, that isn't how the rules work here — the permanents enter simultaneously.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same with more than two players; every player in turn order after the active player chooses their card knowing the earlier choices, and the same APNAP ordering governs the enters-the-battlefield choices (rules 101.4b, 616.1f).

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
Yes — after the equip resolves, Wandering Ones has flying.

Why: Tightening Coils' effect ("enchanted creature loses flying") and Fleetfeather Sandals' effect ("equipped creature has flying and haste") both apply in layer 6, the layer for ability-adding and ability-removing effects [613.1f]. Neither depends on the other, so they're applied in timestamp order, and the later one wins [613.9]. While Tightening Coils was cast after Fleetfeather Sandals was already attached, Tightening Coils had the later timestamp, so Wandering Ones had no flying.

When Adriel activates Fleetfeather Sandals' equip ability and it resolves, Fleetfeather Sandals becomes attached to Wandering Ones anew, and the continuous effects generated by its static abilities receive new timestamps (this is the same principle illustrated in the Colossus Hammer/Rune of Flight example: when the Equipment becomes attached to a creature, its abilities receive new timestamps) [613.7a]. Fleetfeather Sandals' grant of flying now has the later timestamp, so in layer 6 it is applied after Tightening Coils' removal, and Wandering Ones ends up with flying (and haste) [613.9], [613.1f]. An Equipment's static ability applies to whatever it is currently attached to and isn't "locked in" [604.4], [611.3a], [301.5f].

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming the equip ability actually resolves and re-attaches Fleetfeather Sandals to Wandering Ones (equipping a creature the Equipment is already attached to is legal; the ability just re-attaches it). If instead Nico were to enchant Wandering Ones with a fresh Tightening Coils after the equip resolves, that new Aura would have the later timestamp and Wandering Ones would lose flying again.

Nothing here depends on the number of players — the layer and timestamp rules work identically in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Addilynn activates the Unearth ability of their [Extractor Demon], returning it to the battlefield. Before their end step, Addilynn casts [Reality Ripple] targeting Extractor Demon. What happens to it?
answer:
Short answer: Extractor Demon ends up exiled permanently, and it does not come back at the beginning of the next end step.

Assumption: I'm treating Reality Ripple as an effect that exiles the target and returns it to the battlefield at the beginning of the next end step (its text wasn't provided in the context — if it does something else, this answer changes).

Why:

1. Unearth gives the returned permanent, among other things, the replacement effect "If it would leave the battlefield, exile it instead of putting it anywhere else" [702.84a]. That replacement is a continuous replacement effect that applies to any zone change off the battlefield, including one caused by Reality Ripple.

2. So when Reality Ripple tries to move Extractor Demon off the battlefield, the unearth replacement applies and Extractor Demon is exiled by the unearth effect rather than by Reality Ripple's own zone change [702.84a], [616.1f].

3. Reality Ripple's return is a delayed triggered ability / second one-shot effect that returns the object it moved [610.3], [603.7c]. Because Extractor Demon didn't leave the battlefield the way that effect specified — the unearth replacement exiled it instead — and because a card that changes zones becomes a new object, the delayed ability finds nothing to return; a delayed triggered ability "won't do anything if the permanent left the battlefield before then" and won't affect an object that isn't the object it's expecting [603.7c].

4. Unearth's own delayed ability ("Exile it at the beginning of the next end step") likewise does nothing, since Extractor Demon already left the battlefield [603.7c], [702.84a].

Net result: Extractor Demon sits in exile as a new object, owned by Addilynn, with no way for either delayed ability to bring it back.

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, and the same result occurs in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Avery controls [Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher] and Natalie controls [Verity Circle] and [Koskun Falls]. Avery attacks Natalie with Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher, and then taps it to pay for the cost required by Koskun Falls. Will Natalie's Verity Circle trigger?
answer:
I can't fully answer this: the provided context contains card data only for Extractor Demon and Reality Ripple, not for Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher, Verity Circle, or Koskun Falls, so I have no authoritative text for the three cards the question actually hinges on.

What the provided rules do settle is that the sequence as described can't happen. During the declare attackers step, the active player taps the chosen attacking creatures, and that tapping "isn't a cost; attacking simply causes creatures to become tapped" [508.1f]. Only after that does the active player choose optional attack costs [508.1g], determine and lock in the total cost to attack [508.1h], and get a chance to activate mana abilities if mana is required [508.1i]. So by the time Avery would pay an attack cost such as tapping a creature, Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher is already tapped from having been declared as an attacker, and "a permanent that's already tapped can't be tapped to pay a cost" [118.3]. Avery would have to tap some other untapped creature — or, if Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher has vigilance or a similar ability keeping it untapped when attacking, it could still be tapped for the cost, but I don't have its text to confirm.

What I'd need to finish the answer: the exact text of Verity Circle (specifically whether it triggers on "becomes tapped" and whether it excludes creatures tapped for attacking), the exact cost wording on Koskun Falls, and whether Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher taps when attacking. Note also that if Avery does successfully tap a creature to pay, rule 118.11/118.7 principles about modified or reduced costs don't change that the cost was paid.

question: Nico controls [Platinum Emperion]. Alexandra attacks with [Hopeful Eidolon], which Nico doesn't block. Does Alexandra gain life?
answer:
Yes — Alexandra gains life equal to the damage Hopeful Eidolon deals. Hopeful Eidolon has lifelink, and lifelink is a static ability under which damage dealt by the source causes that source's controller (Alexandra) to gain that much life, in addition to any other results of the damage [702.15a, 702.15b, 120.3f]. The life gain is a real life-gain event, so Alexandra's life total is adjusted upward and any "whenever you gain life" triggers she controls will trigger [119.3, 119.9].

The key point: lifelink gives life to the source's controller, not to the damaged player. Platinum Emperion is Nico's permanent and it only locks down Nico's own life total, so it does nothing to stop Alexandra's gain. Note also that damage dealt to a player by a source without infect causes that player to lose life [120.3a] — that life loss is what Platinum Emperion interferes with on Nico's side; it is a separate result from Alexandra's life gain, and one being stopped doesn't stop the other [120.3f, 120.4d].

Caveat: the exact oracle text of Platinum Emperion and Hopeful Eidolon wasn't supplied in my context, so I'm relying on the general lifelink rules and on Platinum Emperion affecting only its controller's life total. If a card's printed text said otherwise, that text would override the general rule.

Multiplayer: the provided rules include only a Two-Headed Giant note that damage, life loss, and life gain happen to each player individually and apply to the team's shared life total [810.9g]. Outside of that team format, the answer is the same at any table size — Alexandra gains the life regardless of how many players are in the game.

question: Ari casts a [Hero of Oxid Ridge]. In response, Nixon casts [Hallow], targeting the Hero of Oxid Ridge. When Ari attacks with the Hero of Oxid Ridge that turn, will the damage be prevented?
answer:
Short answer: the provided rules don't settle this one, so I can't give you a definitive yes/no.

What's missing is the rule governing what happens when a damage-prevention "shield" is aimed at a source that is currently a spell on the stack (Hero of Oxid Ridge as a spell) and that spell then resolves and becomes a permanent "a new object". That rule (the part of 609.7 about choosing a source that's a spell, and about objects changing zones becoming new objects) is not in the context I was given, and Hallow's own oracle text wasn't supplied either.

What the provided rules do tell us:
- A prevention effect is a continuous "shield" that watches for a damage event and prevents some or all of it; it is not locked in when created [615.1a].
- When a shield applies to damage "from a source," the shield rechecks the source's properties at the moment damage would be dealt. If the properties no longer match, no damage is prevented and the shield isn't used up [609.7b, 615.9].
- If combat damage from Hero of Oxid Ridge were fully prevented, it would simply never happen, and any ability that triggers on that damage being dealt wouldn't trigger [615.6, 603.2g].

So the outcome turns entirely on whether the Hallow shield, created while Hero of Oxid Ridge was still a spell, still "matches" Hero of Oxid Ridge once it is a creature on the battlefield attacking. I'd need the rule on spells becoming permanents (new objects) or Hallow's exact text to answer that, and I won't guess.

Timing note: I'm assuming Hallow resolved while Hero of Oxid Ridge was still on the stack (that's what "in response" implies). If instead Hallow were cast after Hero of Oxid Ridge had already resolved and was on the battlefield, the source chosen would be the permanent itself, and its combat damage that turn would be prevented [615.1a, 615.6].

Multiplayer note: the rules given cover only the ordinary case plus a multiplayer range-of-influence caveat "a prevention effect can only affect sources and recipients within its controller's range of influence [801.13b]" which matters only in formats with a limited range of influence, not in a normal two-player or free-for-all game.

Prevention effects that apply to damage from a permanent spell on the stack continue to apply to damage from the permanent that spell becomes.

Such effects watch for a damage event that would happen and completely or partially prevent the damage that would be dealt. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “prevent” are prevention effects. Prevention effects use “prevent” to indicate what damage will not be dealt.

An ability that triggers on damage being dealt won’t trigger if all the damage is prevented.

question: Ariel wants to participate in a sanctioned Magic tournament, but doesn't know where to find one. To which section of the comprehensive rules should they refer?
answer: Ariel should look at rule 100.6 — specifically 100.6b — in section 1 ("Game Concepts") of the Comprehensive Rules. Rule 100.6b states that players can use the Magic Store & Event Locator at Locator.Wizards.com to find tournaments in their area. That same rule also notes that most Magic tournaments (organized play activities where players compete against other players to win prizes) have additional rules covered in the Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules, found at WPN.Wizards.com/en/rules-documents, which may limit the use of some cards, including barring all cards from some older sets [100.6, 100.6b]. So rule 100.6 tells Ariel both where to find an event and where to find the extra rules that will govern it.

question: Arjun's [Morality Shift] resolves, in what order do they put cards in their graveyard?
answer:
Direct answer: the owner of the cards chooses the order. Whenever an effect or rule puts two or more cards into the same graveyard at the same time, that graveyard's owner may arrange them in any order they like [404.3]. So when Morality Shift resolves and Arjun's library is put into Arjun's graveyard as a single simultaneous event, Arjun arranges those cards in any order he chooses — no other player has input, and the choice is made as the cards are put there, not later.

Once they're there, the graveyard is a single face-up pile that anyone may examine at any time, but its order can't normally be changed afterward (some sanctioned-tournament floor rules do permit reordering your own graveyard) [404.2].

Assumption and caveat: I wasn't given Morality Shift's oracle text, so I'm assuming it moves the cards into the graveyard all at once. If instead the card moved them one at a time, each card would simply be placed on top as it arrived and 404.3 wouldn't grant a free arrangement. Also note that if the same effect grouped cards into piles first, cards in piles don't leave the zone they're in, and any graveyard order must be maintained during that process [700.3c].

Multiplayer: this is unchanged with more than two players, since only the owner makes the arrangement choice; if some other simultaneous action required choices from several players, those would be made in APNAP order (active player first, then the others in turn order) and then happen simultaneously [101.4].

question: Audrey casts [Enlarge] targeting [Goblin Piker], and then attacks with the Goblin Piker. Nico blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Grafted Exoskeleton] and indestructible due to their [Withstand Death]. What happens at the end of the turn?
answer:
Goblin Piker dies in the cleanup step; Baron Sengir survives.

How it plays out:

1. Combat damage. Baron Sengir has infect from Grafted Exoskeleton, so the damage Baron Sengir deals to Goblin Piker isn't marked on Goblin Piker at all — instead Nico puts that many -1/-1 counters on Goblin Piker [702.90c]. (If Baron Sengir had dealt damage to a player instead, it would give poison counters rather than causing life loss [702.90b].) Goblin Piker, pumped by Enlarge, survives combat because the -1/-1 counters don't reduce its toughness to 0 while the +X/+X boost is active.
2. Goblin Piker's damage to Baron Sengir is marked as normal damage, but Withstand Death makes Baron Sengir indestructible, so lethal marked damage doesn't destroy it.
3. Cleanup step. All damage marked on permanents is removed and all "until end of turn"/"this turn" effects end simultaneously [514.2], [500.5a]. That ends Enlarge's power/toughness boost. The -1/-1 counters, however, are counters, not an "until end of turn" effect — they stay on Goblin Piker.
4. Characteristics are recalculated: Goblin Piker's printed power/toughness with the Enlarge boost gone, then the -1/-1 counters applied in layer 7 [613.1g]. Because the counters were sized to match the boosted Goblin Piker, its toughness is now 0 or less, and state-based actions put Goblin Piker into its owner's graveyard [704.5f]. Goblin Piker is not indestructible, and even indestructibility wouldn't save it — 0-or-less toughness isn't destruction [704.5f].

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Enlarge resolved before blockers and combat damage, and that its effect lasts "until end of turn." If instead the pump had already expired before damage (it can't here, but for contrast), Baron Sengir's infect counters would likely have killed Goblin Piker during combat via the same state-based action.

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes with more than two players — the cleanup step and state-based actions work identically regardless of player count; only Audrey's Goblin Piker is affected.

question: Ariel activates [Warped Landscape]. Before that resolves Noe casts [Aven Mindcensor]. When Ariel is resolving Warped Landscape's ability, they find [Panglacial Wurm] in the top four cards of their library. Can they cast it?
answer:
Yes — Ariel can cast Panglacial Wurm, provided Panglacial Wurm is among the top four cards Aven Mindcensor restricts the search to (which the question states it is).

Why: Aven Mindcensor doesn't stop the search; it replaces searching the library with searching only the top four cards of that library. Rule [701.23f] says that when searching a zone is replaced with searching a portion of that zone, any other instructions that refer to searching the zone still apply. Panglacial Wurm's own text lets you cast it from your library while you're searching your library, so that permission still functions during the reduced search — but only for the cards actually being searched. If Panglacial Wurm had been the fifth card down or deeper, Ariel would never see it and couldn't cast it.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Aven Mindcensor resolved and was on the battlefield at the moment Warped Landscape's ability began resolving and the search started; that's what makes its replacement effect apply to Ariel's search. If Aven Mindcensor somehow entered after the search had already begun, it wouldn't alter that search at all, and Ariel could look at their whole library and still cast Panglacial Wurm from it.

Ariel still has to pay Panglacial Wurm's full mana cost and follow normal timing permissions granted by its own text; casting it happens in the middle of the search, and the search then continues afterward. Note also that Warped Landscape's search instruction (and any shuffle instruction attached to it) still applies in full — per the Veteran Explorer example in [701.23f], a shuffle instruction shuffles the entire library, not just the four searched cards.

Multiplayer: this works the same at any table size. Aven Mindcensor's restriction applies to each of its controller's opponents, so whether the game has two players or more, Ariel's search is cut to the top four and Panglacial Wurm remains castable from among those four.

question: Addison has cast a sideboard card from [Glittering Wish], which is now in their graveyard. Addison then restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
answer:
The sideboard card Addison brought into the game with Glittering Wish becomes part of Addison's starting deck in the new game — it shuffles into their library when the restarted game begins, even though it started outside the game.

Why: a game that is restarted immediately ends, no one wins, loses, or draws it, and all players who were in the game when it ended start a new game following the normal starting-the-game procedure [727.1], [104.6]. All Magic cards involved in the ended game are involved in the new game, including cards that weren't originally part of it — the rules give exactly this example: a card brought in from outside the game by a wish effect (Living Wish there, Glittering Wish here) will be part of that player's library when the new game begins, no matter what zone it was in (here, Addison's graveyard) when the game ended [727.2]. Ownership doesn't change, so it goes into Addison's library specifically [727.2].

Note that "outside the game" isn't a zone; sideboard cards are outside the game [400.11a], and normally sideboards are set aside before the starting deck is fixed [103.2a]. Rule 727.2 overrides that for a restart: the wished-for card is now part of the deck. The only cards that don't join the new deck are ones an effect specifically exempts from the restart procedure (for example, the card that restarts the game itself typically exempts itself) [727.5]. The restarting effect finishes resolving just before the first turn's untap step, and any additional instructions on it are carried out then [727.4].

Multiplayer: this works the same regardless of the number of players — every player still in the game when it restarts begins the new game [727.1], [104.6]. The only special case is a Magic subgame: if a subgame were restarted, the main game would be unaffected [727.6].

question: Alvin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], a [Dance of the Dead] attached to a [Streetbreaker Wurm] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Alvin casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield, then putting [Copy Artifact] onto the battlefield, which copies the Mizzium Transreliquat and then copies the Dance of the Dead with its new copy ability. (The one from Sakashima of a Thousand Faces.) They choose for it to enchant a [Viashino Warrior] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines. After Copy Artifact's trigger resolves and returns the Viashino Warrior to the battlefield, Alvin activates the ability of the Copy Artifact to turn it into a copy of Streetbreaker Wurm. What happens?
answer:
I can't answer this reliably from what's provided — the provided context doesn't include the card text for Mycosynth Lattice, Dance of the Dead, Streetbreaker Wurm, Mizzium Transreliquat, Sakashima of a Thousand Faces, Copy Artifact (beyond a passing mention), Eureka, March of the Machines, Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked, or Viashino Warrior. Every step of this puzzle hinges on the exact wording of those cards (especially Dance of the Dead's "enchant creature card in a graveyard" / return-and-attach ability and its clause about being sacrificed if it stops enchanting the creature, and Mizzium Transreliquat's copy ability), and I'm not permitted to supply that wording from outside the context.

What the provided rules do establish, in case it helps you work it through once you have the card texts in hand:

- A permanent that copies another permanent takes only the copiable values (name, mana cost, card types, subtypes, rules text, power/toughness, etc.), as modified by other copy effects and by its own status; type-changing effects (such as those from Mycosynth Lattice or March of the Machines), counters, and other noncopy effects are not copied [707.2], [707.3].
- When a permanent already on the battlefield changes what it's copying, that change does not trigger enters-the-battlefield or leaves-the-battlefield abilities, and noncopy effects currently affecting it keep applying [707.4].
- A copy effect that says "except it has this ability" makes that granted ability part of the copy's new copiable values, so later copies of it pick that ability up too [707.9a], [707.9b].
- An ability a copy gains that names a card is read as naming the object it's now on, per the name-substitution rule [201.5b], and effects that refer to a permanent by name keep tracking that permanent even after it becomes a copy of something else [707.11].
- If several replacement effects (including copy-as-it-enters effects) want to apply to the same entering permanent, the affected permanent's controller picks the order, re-checking after each application [616.1f].

What's missing to finish the ruling: the actual text of Dance of the Dead (including its "enchanted creature" and sacrifice/exile clauses), Mizzium Transreliquat's activated abilities, Copy Artifact's exact wording, and Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' copy ability. Without those I'd be guessing at the outcome, which I won't do.

question: Aspen controls a [Blood Tyrant] that they took control of from Briella using [Malevolent Whispers]. Aspen has 1 life. Cason casts [Volt Charge] targeting Aspen. After it resolves and Aspen loses the game, will Blood Tyrant get the +1/+1 counters?
answer:
Short answer: No — Blood Tyrant won't end up with counters from Aspen's own loss under Aspen's control, and with Aspen out of the game there is no controller left for that triggered ability.

How the pieces fit, with the rules provided:

1. Aspen at 1 life taking damage from Cason's Volt Charge is reduced to 0 or less life, and Aspen loses the game as a state-based action [119.6], [704.8].

2. Abilities that trigger "when a player loses the game" trigger regardless of the reason [603.9], and they are on the short list of abilities that "look back in time" — the game uses the existence of those abilities and the appearance of the objects as they were immediately before the event [603.10f]. So the fact that Blood Tyrant was, at the moment of the loss, a permanent Aspen controlled (via Malevolent Whispers' control-change effect) is what's used.

3. But when Aspen leaves the game, the control-change effect from Malevolent Whispers ends immediately and Blood Tyrant reverts to Briella's control; this is not a state-based action and happens as soon as Aspen leaves [800.4a]. At the same time, any objects on the stack not represented by cards that Aspen controlled (which is what a triggered ability on the stack is) cease to exist, and any other objects still controlled by Aspen are exiled [800.4a]. A triggered ability that would be controlled by the departing player Aspen therefore doesn't get to resolve, so Blood Tyrant receives no counters from Aspen's loss.

Player count: three players are named (Aspen, Briella, Cason), so this is a multiplayer game and play continues after Aspen leaves [800.4a]. In a two-player game the loss of one player simply ends the game, so nothing resolves at all.

One gap you should know about: I was not given the oracle text of Blood Tyrant, Malevolent Whispers, or Volt Charge. If Blood Tyrant's own printed text specifies something different (for example, who controls or benefits from the loss trigger, or a fixed number of counters), that printed text overrides the general rules above — I can't verify its wording from the context provided.

Timing note: I assumed Volt Charge finished resolving and then the state-based action check found Aspen at 0 or less life. If instead something restored Aspen's life before state-based actions were checked, Aspen never loses and the loss trigger never happens at all.

question: Aspen, Brycen, and Collins begin a multiplayer game. In Aspen's upkeep, they use [Leyline of Anticipation], several [Simian Spirit Guide]s and [Desperate Ritual]s, and [Goblin Charbelcher] to kill Brycen. Does Aspen draw a card for the turn?
answer:
Yes. Aspen draws a card during their draw step.

Why: Brycen leaving the game doesn't end the game here, because Aspen still has an opponent — Collins. A player only wins immediately when *all* of that player's opponents have left the game [104.2a]. With Collins still in, play continues; multiplayer games can keep going after one or more players have left [800.4k].

Aspen's turn is already underway (the kill happened in Aspen's upkeep), so the upkeep step ends and the draw step begins normally. Immediately after the draw step begins, the active player — Aspen — draws a card as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [504.1] [703.4d]. And since this is the first turn of a multiplayer game, the usual "starting player skips their first draw step" rule does not apply: in multiplayer games other than two-player, no player skips the draw step of their first turn [103.8c]. So even if Aspen is the starting player on turn one, Aspen draws.

Contrast with two players: if Brycen had been Aspen's only opponent, Aspen would have won the game immediately upon Brycen leaving [104.2a], and there would be no draw step to reach. Note also that Brycen leaving the game because of lethal damage (not a draw) can trigger abilities that trigger on a player losing the game [603.9].

Timing note: I'm assuming Brycen is killed during Aspen's upkeep step, as stated, and that Aspen's draw step follows. If somehow Goblin Charbelcher's damage were dealt after Aspen's draw step had already been passed, the draw would simply already have happened.
