No — Addison will not draw a card during the first turn of the restarted game.

Why: Karn Liberated's restart ends the current game immediately and the players *still in the game* at that moment begin a new game [104.6][727.1]. Collins had already lost, so Collins is not part of the restarted game — only Addison and Brixton are. That makes the new game a two-player game.

Addison is the starting player of the new game, because the starting player is the player who controlled the spell or ability that restarted the game [727.1a]. In a two-player game, the player who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn [103.8a]. So Addison, as the starting player in what is now a two-player game, skips the draw step and draws nothing on turn one.

Contrast with a still-multiplayer restart: if Collins were still in the game (three or more players), no player would skip the draw step of their first turn [103.8c][800.7], and Addison would draw during their first turn's draw step as a turn-based action [504.1][703.4d]. question: Aniyah casts [Martyrdom], targeting their [Douser of Lights]. After it resolves, Nico takes control of Douser of Lights with [Act of Aggression]. Can Nico activate the ability it gained from Martyrdom?
answer:
Yes — Nico can activate it, because the ability now belongs to Douser of Lights itself, and activated abilities of a permanent are activated by that permanent's controller.

Why: Martyrdom's effect grants ("gains") an activated ability to the object Douser of Lights; an effect that adds an ability makes that ability part of the object, along with any activation instructions the effect included [113.10a]. Whoever has priority may activate the activated abilities of permanents they control [117.1b], so once Act of Aggression gives Nico control of Douser of Lights, Nico is the player who can activate the granted ability, not Aniyah. This mirrors the Aura principle in [303.4e]: when an effect grants an ability to an object with "gains" or "has," only the enchanted/granted object's controller can activate that ability.

Caveats:
- Any restriction printed as part of the granted ability (e.g. "activate only once each turn," or a {T} cost) still travels with it and applies to Nico [602.5b] [602.5c]. In particular, if the granted ability has {T} or {Q} in its cost, Nico can't activate it unless Douser of Lights has haste or has been under Nico's control since the start of Nico's most recent turn [602.5a]; Act of Aggression grants haste, which solves that.
- A player can't activate abilities of an object outside their range of influence, which matters only in formats with such a range [801.6].
- I'm assuming the granted ability lasts "until end of turn" and that the control change happens while it's still granted; if Martyrdom's grant had already expired, there'd be no ability to activate. Note also that if the granted ability's effect refers to "this creature's controller" or similar, that will now be Nico.
- This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of players.

One gap: Martyrdom's exact oracle text wasn't provided, so I can't tell you what the ability actually does or what its cost is — only who may activate it.

question: Ashley has restarted the game with a [Karn Liberated] that exiled an [Ajani's Chosen]. Ashley chooses to begin the restarted game with a [Leyline of Anticipation] on the battlefield. Does Ajani's Chosen trigger?
answer:
No — Ajani's Chosen doesn't trigger, because Leyline of Anticipation enters the battlefield before Ajani's Chosen does.

Sequence:

1. The game restarts. Cards exiled by Karn Liberated are exempted from the restart procedure, so Ajani's Chosen is not in Ashley's deck as the new game begins [727.5].
2. The new game is set up per rule 103, and during the opening-hand actions — after mulligans, before the first turn — Ashley puts Leyline of Anticipation onto the battlefield [103.6a]. At that moment Ajani's Chosen is still in exile, so there is nothing on the battlefield with the "whenever an enchantment enters, create a Cat" ability. Trigger conditions are checked against the objects and continuous effects that exist immediately after the event [603.10a], and Ajani's Chosen isn't among them.
3. The restart effect finishes resolving just before the first turn's untap step, and the additional instructions of the ability that restarted the game (Karn Liberated returning its exiled non-Aura permanent cards to the battlefield) are carried out at that time. No player has priority, and anything that does trigger then waits to go on the stack until the first upkeep step [727.4].

So Ajani's Chosen arrives strictly later than Leyline of Anticipation, and an "enters" trigger only sees enters-the-battlefield events that happen while the triggering permanent is already there. Ajani's Chosen would trigger on the *next* enchantment that enters.

Timing caveat: this rests on Leyline of Anticipation being put onto the battlefield during the opening-hand step of the new game, which is where rule 103.6a places it. If instead you imagine both hitting the battlefield simultaneously, Ajani's Chosen still wouldn't trigger, since a permanent's enters-the-battlefield-triggered ability doesn't trigger on permanents entering at the same time as it.

Multiplayer: the same answer applies. Restarting includes all players who were in the game when it ended, and in a multiplayer game using the limited range of influence option every player is involved regardless of range of influence [727.7]; that doesn't change the ordering above.

question: Arden controls [Naga Vitalist] and a [Deathrite Shaman] that's currently a land due to [Xenograft] (naming "Saproling") and [Life and Limb]. Neither player has any land cards in their graveyards. If Arden taps Naga Vitalist, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Naga Vitalist can only produce {G}.

Why: Deathrite Shaman is a Saproling because of Xenograft (naming "Saproling"), and Life and Limb makes all Saprolings and all Forests both 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands, so Deathrite Shaman is a land with the basic land type Forest. Any land with the Forest subtype has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {G}" [305.6][Forest], so that is a type of mana a land Arden controls could produce.

Deathrite Shaman's own first ability (exile a target land card from a graveyard: add one mana of any color) does not widen the options here. Determining what a permanent "could produce" asks what type of mana an ability of that permanent would produce if it resolved at that time, ignoring only whether the costs could be paid [106.7]. With no land cards in any graveyard there is no legal target, so that ability wouldn't resolve and produce mana at all; no type of mana is defined by it, and an ability that would produce mana of an undefined type produces none [106.5]. (It's still a mana ability regardless — being unable to produce mana doesn't change that [605.2].)

So Naga Vitalist's mana ability sees exactly one available type, {G}, and adds one {G}. Note {G} is green mana specifically, not generic {1} and not colorless {C}.

Assumption/timing note: I'm assuming nothing changes graveyard contents between now and when the ability resolves. Naga Vitalist's ability is a mana ability, so it resolves immediately without being put on the stack; if a land card were somehow in a graveyard at that moment, Deathrite Shaman "could produce" any color and Naga Vitalist could then add mana of any of the five colors.

Multiplayer difference: the question says "neither player," which frames a two-player game. Deathrite Shaman's ability targets a land card in *a* graveyard, not just an opponent's, so at a table with more than two players, a land card in any other player's graveyard would make Deathrite Shaman able to produce any color, and Naga Vitalist could then add {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G}.

I don't have Naga Vitalist's, Xenograft's, or Life and Limb's card text in the provided context, so the above relies on the type-changing setup as you described it.

question: Ashley controls [Skill Borrower] and [Sensei's Divining Top]. The top card of their library is a [Putrid Leech]. Ashley activates Skill Borrower's ability, then activates Sensei's Divining Top's first ability, choosing to put Putrid Leech second from the top. Then they activate Sensei's Divining Top again, putting Putrid Leech back on top. Can Ashley activate Skill Borrower's ability again?
answer:
Yes. Because Putrid Leech left the top-of-library "revealed" position and then came back, it is a new object, and the once-per-turn restriction on the ability Skill Borrower granted from the earlier object doesn't carry over to the ability granted by the new object.

Why:

1. Skill Borrower gives itself the activated abilities of the top card of Ashley's library, and Ashley plays with that top card revealed. Rule 401.6 says that if a card being played with revealed stops being revealed for any length of time and is then revealed again, it becomes a new object. Putting Putrid Leech second from the top with Sensei's Divining Top and then returning it to the top with the second Sensei's Divining Top activation does exactly that, so the Putrid Leech now on top is a new object, not the same one Skill Borrower was drawing the ability from before.

2. Rule 602.5c says that when an object acquires an activated ability that carries a restriction on its use from another object, that restriction applies only to that ability as acquired from that object — it does not apply to other, identically worded abilities. The "activate only once each turn" style restriction that came with the first Putrid Leech object therefore doesn't restrict the identically worded ability Skill Borrower now has from the new Putrid Leech object. Ashley can activate it again this turn.

Timing note: rule 401.5 matters if the top card changes in the middle of activating something — the new top card isn't revealed and can't be looked at until the activation is complete. So Ashley must finish activating the first ability (and finish each Sensei's Divining Top activation) before the newly revealed Putrid Leech's ability is available. I'm assuming the sequence in the question happened cleanly one activation at a time; if instead Ashley tried to respond to their own Skill Borrower activation by shuffling the top card around and then "re-choosing" the granted ability mid-activation, that wouldn't work — the already-announced activation is locked in.

One caveat: the exact wording of Skill Borrower, Sensei's Divining Top, and Putrid Leech was not provided in my context, so this answer rests on the general rules above (401.6 and 602.5c) rather than on their card text. If Putrid Leech's restriction were worded to track the player rather than the ability, the outcome could differ.

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on how many opponents are at the table, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and in multiplayer.

question: Ariel attacks with [Wildfire Eternal], which isn't blocked. As the trigger resolves, can they choose to suspend [Charnel Serenade]?
answer:
No — Ariel can't suspend Charnel Serenade during the resolution of Wildfire Eternal's triggered ability.

Why: Suspending a card is a *special action*, not casting a spell. Rule 116.2f lists exiling a card with suspend from your hand as one of the twelve special actions, and rule 702.62a spells out the suspend static ability as "If you could begin to cast this card by putting it onto the stack from your hand, you may pay [cost] and exile it with N time counters on it. This action doesn't use the stack." Special actions don't use the stack; they happen immediately (405.6d), and a player may take that suspend action only when they have priority (116.2f). No player has priority in the middle of a spell or ability resolving, so there is no window to suspend Charnel Serenade "as the trigger resolves."

Separately, an effect that lets you *cast* a card lets you cast it — it doesn't let you take the suspend special action instead. Suspend's third ability (702.62a) is what later lets you play the suspended card once the last time counter is removed; the suspend cost itself is paid via the special action, not by casting.

What Ariel can do: after Wildfire Eternal's trigger finishes resolving and Ariel receives priority again, they may take the suspend special action on Charnel Serenade, provided they could begin to cast it from hand at that time (702.62a, 702.62c — you must account for any effect prohibiting casting it).

One caveat on the facts: the context doesn't include Wildfire Eternal's or Charnel Serenade's card text, so I'm answering the general question of whether suspend can be taken during a trigger's resolution. Also note your description has the trigger resolving from the attack; if the trigger in question actually triggers on combat damage instead, the answer is unchanged. This reasoning is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since priority rules for special actions don't vary by player count.

question: Brynn has 1 life and controls a phased-out [Fairgrounds Warden] that exiled Coleman's [Alpha Tyrranax]. Aspen casts [Psychic Purge], targeting Brynn. What happens as Brynn loses the game?
answer:
Alpha Tyrranax stays in exile forever. Because the Fairgrounds Warden that exiled it was phased out when Brynn left the game, the Fairgrounds Warden leaves the game without ever "leaving the battlefield," so its return trigger never happens.

Details:

1. Brynn is reduced to 0 or less life by Psychic Purge and loses the game (I'm assuming Psychic Purge's damage/loss-of-life finishes Brynn off at 1 life). Any triggered abilities that trigger on a player losing the game do trigger and use the "look back in time" rule, checking the game state as it existed immediately before Brynn left [603.9] [603.10f].

2. As soon as Brynn leaves, every object Brynn owns leaves the game; this is not a state-based action and doesn't use the stack [800.4a] [405.6h]. Phased-out permanents owned by that player also leave the game, and rule [702.26k] states explicitly that this does not cause zone-change abilities to trigger.

3. "Phased out" means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist for most game purposes. Critically, the glossary entry for Leaves the Battlefield says a permanent leaves the battlefield when it leaves the game because its owner left the game only if it's phased in [Leaves the Battlefield]. The Fairgrounds Warden was phased out, so it never "leaves the battlefield," and the exile effect keyed to "when Fairgrounds Warden leaves the battlefield" has no event to trigger on. Alpha Tyrranax remains exiled permanently, even though Coleman is still in the game (Coleman owns it, so it doesn't leave the game with Brynn).

4. Compare: had the Fairgrounds Warden been phased in, its leaving the game would have counted as leaving the battlefield and Alpha Tyrranax would have returned.

5. This whole scenario is a multiplayer one (three named players), and it only works because multiplayer games continue after a player leaves [800.4a]. In a two-player game, Brynn's loss would simply end the game, so the question of Alpha Tyrranax returning would be moot.

Timing note: if instead Psychic Purge resolved without reducing Brynn to 0 and Brynn lost later for another reason, the outcome is identical — what matters is only that the Fairgrounds Warden was phased out at the moment Brynn left the game. If the Fairgrounds Warden had phased in before Brynn left, Alpha Tyrranax would return to the battlefield under Coleman's control.

question: Avery controls [Caelorna, Coral Tyrant] and [Darksteel Garrison] that's fortifying [Spire Garden]. Avery casts [Bludgeon Brawl]. After that resolves they activate Darksteel Garrison's equip ability targeting Caelorna, Coral Tyrant. What does the battlefield look like after that ability has resolved and state-based actions have been checked?
answer:
After the equip ability resolves, Darksteel Garrison is attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant (equipping it) and is no longer fortifying Spire Garden; Spire Garden is left on the battlefield unfortified, and state-based actions don't detach anything.

Why: attaching is a move, not an addition — the equip ability attaches Darksteel Garrison to the target creature, so it stops being attached to Spire Garden. Darksteel Garrison is normally an artifact Fortification, but with Bludgeon Brawl's effect applied it is also an Equipment with an equip ability, and an Equipment may legally be attached to a creature; since Caelorna, Coral Tyrant is a creature, the attachment is legal and no state-based action pulls it off (301.5c: an Equipment that equips an illegal or nonexistent permanent becomes unattached, which isn't the case here; it also isn't equipping more than one creature). Note that 704.5p only unattaches a noncreature, nonbattle permanent that is neither an Aura, an Equipment, nor a Fortification — Darksteel Garrison is both an Equipment and a Fortification, so 704.5p leaves it attached. Caelorna, Coral Tyrant is now "modified," since it is equipped (see the Modified glossary entry), and it gains whatever bonus Bludgeon Brawl's granted "equipped creature" ability provides plus Darksteel Garrison's own equipped-creature effects.

Two assumptions worth flagging: (1) Bludgeon Brawl's own text wasn't provided here, so I'm relying on it being what makes Darksteel Garrison an Equipment with equip — if it didn't grant Equipment status and an equip ability, there would be no equip ability to activate at all. (2) I'm assuming the equip was activated after Bludgeon Brawl had resolved, as stated; if Bludgeon Brawl were somehow no longer applying when the ability resolved, Darksteel Garrison would lose the Equipment subtype and 301.5c would make it unattach from Caelorna, Coral Tyrant while remaining on the battlefield (it would not go back to fortifying Spire Garden).

Multiplayer difference: none in a two-player game, but at a table of three or more, 801.9 adds that a Fortification can't fortify, and an Equipment can't equip, an object outside its controller's range of influence; if Caelorna, Coral Tyrant were outside Avery's range of influence, Darksteel Garrison would become unattached as a state-based action and stay on the battlefield.

Darksteel Garrison is attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant and not to Spire Garden.

question: Noah controls a [Mons's Goblin Raiders] enchanted with a [Spider Umbra]. Alexandra casts [Yamabushi's Flame], targeting Mons's Goblin Raiders. What happens?
answer:
Mons's Goblin Raiders survives; Spider Umbra is destroyed instead. Yamabushi's Flame's 3 damage is lethal to the 2/2 Mons's Goblin Raiders (1/1 plus Spider Umbra's bonus), so it would be destroyed — but Spider Umbra's umbra armor replaces that: "If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura" [702.89a]. So all damage is removed from Mons's Goblin Raiders and Spider Umbra goes to Noah's graveyard.

Details:
- Umbra armor applies whether the creature would be destroyed by lethal damage or by a "destroy" effect; the effect is mandatory [Felidar Umbra ruling #5], [Felidar Umbra ruling #3]. Here it's the game's lethal-damage rules, not Yamabushi's Flame, that cause Spider Umbra to be destroyed [Felidar Umbra ruling #7].
- Because the damage is removed rather than left marked, Mons's Goblin Raiders is fine even after it loses Spider Umbra's +1/+1 and becomes a 1/1 again — it has no damage marked on it, so no state-based action destroys it. Note that umbra armor would not help if Mons's Goblin Raiders' toughness were reduced to 0 or less; a creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner's graveyard [704.5f], [Felidar Umbra ruling #8].
- Umbra armor is not regeneration, so Mons's Goblin Raiders is not tapped and is not removed from combat if this happens during combat [Felidar Umbra ruling #6].

Assumption on timing: damage is dealt and processed into its result all at once during Yamabushi's Flame's resolution, and umbra armor applies as that result is being processed [120.4c]. Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

One caveat: Yamabushi's Flame's own text was not provided in the context. If it contains a clause replacing the creature's death with exile, that clause would only matter if Mons's Goblin Raiders actually died, which it doesn't here — but I can't verify that text from the provided material, and a card's own printed text would override general rules if it said otherwise.

answer_gold:
Spider Umbra is destroyed and Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield.

There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the same event. Umbra armor is attempting to replace the destruction of the creature, while Yamabushi's Flame's effect is attempting to replace where the creature moves to. The "move to the graveyard" event is a part of the "destroy" event, so the umbra armor replacement effect must apply first. Once that effect has been applied, the creature is no longer about to die, so there are no more effects to apply.

If the Mons's Goblin Raiders would die later in the turn, the Yamabushi's Flame's replacement effect will apply at that time and cause it to move to exile instead of the graveyard.

question: Abel attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Murder]?
answer:
I can't settle this from the material provided. The context I was given contains no card data for Pristine Angel, Cephalid Snitch, or Murder, and none of the numbered rules provided cover how a "loses protection from black until end of turn" effect interacts with a protection ability that only applies while a permanent is untapped.

What's missing specifically:
- Pristine Angel's oracle text (in particular the exact wording and duration of its protection/colorless-while-untapped ability).
- Cephalid Snitch's oracle text (what exactly its ability removes and for how long).
- Murder's oracle text (its color and target restriction).
- Rules on continuous effects, layers, and how an effect that removes an ability interacts with an ability that is conditional on the permanent's tapped/untapped state.

The only related rules I was given concern targeting legality on resolution (608.2b), that tapping or untapping a creature already declared as an attacker doesn't remove it from combat (506.4b), and that effects referring to "this/that" object keep applying even if the object's characteristics change (700.7, 608.2k, 603.7c). Those don't resolve whether Pristine Angel regains protection from black upon untapping, so I won't guess. Note also that legality of a target is checked both when Murder is cast and again as Murder resolves (608.2b), so whatever the correct protection answer is, it must hold at both moments.

Also, since the question names only Abel and Nico, I'm treating this as a two-player situation; nothing in the provided rules would change the analysis at a multiplayer table, and no multiplayer-specific rule was supplied.

question: At the beginning of the game, Alex announced [Kaheera, the Orphanguard] as their companion. During the game, Alex cast [Carrion Grub] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alex restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
answer:
Short answer: both Carrion Grub and Kaheera, the Orphanguard are now part of the new game — Carrion Grub (and Kaheera, the Orphanguard, if it had already been moved into the game) starts the new game shuffled into Alex's library — and the provided rules do not cover whether Alex may again designate Kaheera, the Orphanguard as a companion for the restarted game.

Details:

1. Restarting. Karn Liberated's ability ends the current game immediately; nobody wins, loses, or draws, and all players then start a new game following the normal starting-the-game procedure [727.1] [104.6]. The restart effect finishes resolving just before the first turn's untap step, and no player has priority at that moment [727.4]. In a multiplayer game every player in the game when it restarted is involved, even under the limited range of influence option [727.7]; with only two players nothing changes.

2. Carrion Grub. Cards that were brought into the game from outside the game (a sideboard/Wish card) are still "involved in the game that was restarted," and rule 727.2 explicitly covers this case: such a card becomes part of its owner's library when the new game begins. So Carrion Grub is shuffled into Alex's library for the new game, even though it was never in Alex's original deck. Ownership doesn't change [727.2].

3. Kaheera, the Orphanguard. If Alex had taken the special action to put Kaheera, the Orphanguard into their hand, it "remains in the game until the game ends" [702.139c]; since it was a card involved in the ended game, it too is part of the new game and would begin the new game in Alex's library under 727.2. If Kaheera, the Orphanguard was still set aside outside the game (never paid for), the provided rules don't address whether it stays set aside as a companion or is treated as a card involved in the game.

4. The deckbuilding-restriction question. A companion ability checks your starting deck, meaning your deck after sideboard cards are set aside [702.139b]. Nothing in the provided rules says whether companions are re-declared at a restart, or whether the new library — which now contains Carrion Grub, a card that would violate Kaheera, the Orphanguard's restriction — is re-checked. I can't answer that part from the context given; that's the missing piece. Note also that rule 727.5/727.5a allow effects to exempt specific cards from the restart procedure (such cards are not in their owner's deck for the new game), but that only applies if some effect explicitly exempts them.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Carrion Grub was cast and had entered the game before Karn Liberated restarted it. If Carrion Grub had never actually been brought in from outside the game, it would simply remain outside the game and 727.2 wouldn't apply to it.

question: Alex controls a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], a [Mycosynth Lattice], and a [Control Magic] that took control of a [Boris Devilboon] from Nico. Alex begins activating the ability of Boris Devilboon and sacrifices Control Magic to help pay the cost. Is this legal? If so, who will control the ability?
answer:
Yes, it's legal, and Alex will control Boris Devilboon's activated ability.

Why it works:

1. Mycosynth Lattice makes every permanent an artifact, so Alex's Control Magic is an artifact and is a legal thing to sacrifice to Krark-Clan Ironworks' ability ("Sacrifice an artifact: Add {C}{C}"), which Alex activates as a mana ability while paying the costs of Boris Devilboon's ability. (Mycosynth Lattice's text isn't in the provided context, so I'm taking the "everything is an artifact" premise from your question.)

2. Activating an ability means putting it on the stack and paying its costs [602.2, 701.2a]. Alex controlled Boris Devilboon at the moment activation began (Control Magic was still on the battlefield then), so Alex was allowed to activate it — only an object's controller may activate its activated ability [602.2].

3. Sacrificing Control Magic mid-payment ends the control-changing effect, so Boris Devilboon goes back to Nico's control (control-changing effects are applied in layer 2, and when the effect ends the permanent reverts) [613.1b]. But that doesn't undo anything: announcements and payments can't be altered after they've been made [602.2]. Losing control of the source after the ability is already on the stack doesn't remove the ability from the stack or make the activation illegal — legality was checked when the activation began.

4. Controller of the ability: "The controller of an activated ability on the stack is the player who activated it" [113.8]. Alex activated it, so Alex controls it and gets its effect (e.g., any token it creates enters under Alex's control), even though Nico now controls Boris Devilboon itself. Boris Devilboon is still tapped from the {T} cost, and Nico gets it back untapping on Nico's turn.

Timing caveat: this assumes the sacrifice happens during the cost-payment step of activating Boris Devilboon's ability. If instead Alex had sacrificed Control Magic first and only then tried to activate Boris Devilboon's ability, the activation would be illegal — Alex would no longer be Boris Devilboon's controller [602.2] — and the game would rewind to before the attempted activation [602.2].

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players; the rules cited are about the activating player and the ability's controller, not about opponents generally.

question: Nico has cast a [Gather Specimens] earlier in the turn. Aiden controls a [Chronatog Totem] that is currently a creature due to its own ability, and casts an [Evil Twin], choosing to have it copy Chronatog Totem. What happens?
answer:
Evil Twin enters the battlefield as a noncreature artifact named Chronatog Totem, under Aiden's control — Gather Specimens doesn't take it, because nothing is entering the battlefield as a creature.

Why: when you copy a permanent, you copy only its copiable values — the values from the printed text (name, mana cost, card type, subtype, rules text, power/toughness, etc.), as modified by other copy effects, face-down status, and "as . . . enters" abilities that set power and toughness. Other effects, including type-changing effects, are not copied [707.2]. Chronatog Totem is a creature only because of a type-changing effect from its own activated ability, and that effect is not part of its copiable values. Rule [707.2] gives exactly this example with Chimeric Staff: after Chimeric Staff has become a 5/5 Construct artifact creature, a Clone that enters as a copy of it is just an artifact, not a 5/5 creature — though the copy does have the animation ability and can be activated later. The same is true here: Evil Twin will have Chronatog Totem's activated ability and Aiden can animate it (paying its cost) after it's on the battlefield.

Evil Twin's "except it has [its destroy ability]" clause is a modification to the copying process; such modifications become part of the copy's copiable values [707.9b], and copiable/copy effects are applied in layer 1a [613.2a]. That doesn't change the type analysis — the exception adds an ability, not the creature type.

Timing/assumption notes: I'm assuming Chronatog Totem is animated at the moment Evil Twin's copy choice is applied (as Evil Twin enters). The answer is the same regardless — even if Chronatog Totem were animated later, the type-changing effect is never copied. I'm also relying on the standard wording of Gather Specimens (creatures that would enter under an opponent's control enter under its controller's control instead); that card's text was not supplied in the context, so if its actual wording covers permanents generally rather than creatures, the outcome would differ. If Aiden later activates Evil Twin's copied animation ability, Evil Twin becomes a creature then, but Gather Specimens only replaces creatures *entering* the battlefield, so it still stays with Aiden.

Multiplayer: the analysis is identical with more than two players — Gather Specimens' redirection would only ever matter for a creature actually entering under an opponent's control, and here no creature enters at all.

question: Albert and Nico are beginning the game and have just drawn 7 cards. Albert has [Serum Powder] in their hand. Does Albert get to know whether Nico is going to mulligan before deciding whether to use Serum Powder's ability?
answer:
It depends on turn order, not on Serum Powder itself. Albert may use Serum Powder's ability at the moment Albert would declare whether to take a mulligan [103.5b]. Mulligan declarations are made in turn order: the starting player declares first, then each other player in turn order [103.5b]. So:

- If Albert is the starting player, Albert must decide about Serum Powder (and about mulliganing) before Nico has declared anything — Albert does not know Nico's choice.
- If Nico is the starting player, Nico declares first, so Albert does know Nico's declaration before using Serum Powder. Note that a declaration is only whether Nico will mulligan; all mulligans are actually taken simultaneously afterward, so Albert won't see Nico's new hand [103.5b].

Also, rule 103.5b explicitly says the "any time you could mulligan" action need not be taken in the first round of mulligans, and that other players may have already made their mulligan declarations by the time the player has the option to perform it. After performing the action, Albert then declares whether to take a mulligan [103.5b].

Multiplayer: with more than two players the same principle applies — everyone after the starting player knows the earlier declarations in turn order [103.5b]. Additionally, in a multiplayer game (and Brawl) a player's first mulligan doesn't count toward cards put on the bottom of the library or the number of mulligans allowed [103.5c][800.6]. In a shared-team-turns game, the starting team declares first, in any order among themselves, and teammates may consult [103.5d][805.3a].

The provided context doesn't include Serum Powder's card text, so this answer covers only the timing/information question, assuming Serum Powder's ability is usable "any time you could mulligan."

Once each player has made a declaration, all players who decided to take mulligans do so at the same time. To take a mulligan, a player shuffles the cards in their hand back into their library, draws a new hand of cards equal to their starting hand size, then puts a number of those cards equal to the number of times that player has taken a mulligan on the bottom of their library in any order. Once a player chooses not to take a mulligan, the remaining cards become that player’s opening hand, and that player may not take any further mulligans. question: Ariana controls [Sen Triplets], which targeted Nico. Nico's hand contains [Rift Sower]. Can either player suspend it? If so, who will cast it once the last time counter is removed?
answer:
Direct answer: only Nico could possibly suspend Rift Sower, never Ariana — and if Sen Triplets stops Nico from casting spells, then neither player can. If Nico does suspend it, Nico is the one who may cast it when the last time counter is removed.

Why:

1) Suspending is a special action, not a cast. Rule 116.2f: "A player who has a card with suspend in their hand may exile that card," and they may do so only if they could begin to cast that card by putting it onto the stack [116.2f, 702.62a]. The card must be in *that player's* hand. Rift Sower is in Nico's hand, not Ariana's, so Ariana cannot take the suspend special action on it even though Sen Triplets lets her play cards from Nico's hand — Sen Triplets grants permission to play, and suspending is expressly not playing/casting the card [702.62a].

2) Nico's ability to suspend depends on whether anything prohibits him from casting. Rule 702.62c: when determining if you could begin to cast a card with suspend, take into account any effects that would prohibit that card from being cast; rule 601.3: a player can begin to cast a spell only if no rule or effect prohibits it. So if Sen Triplets' effect prohibits Nico from casting spells, Nico cannot satisfy the "could begin to cast" condition and cannot exile Rift Sower with suspend either. Caveat: Sen Triplets' and Rift Sower's actual card text were not provided to me, so I can't confirm from the given materials that Sen Triplets contains a casting prohibition; I'm giving you the rules test to apply to whatever its printed text says. A card's own text overrides general rules where they conflict.

3) Who casts it later. The third suspend ability reads "When the last time counter is removed from this card, if it's exiled, you may play it without paying its mana cost if able" [702.62a]. The "you" is the player who exiled it with suspend — Nico. Nico would be the caster and controller of the resulting spell [112.2a]. Ariana does not get to cast it off Sen Triplets, because at that point Rift Sower is in exile, not in Nico's hand. If it's a creature spell cast this way it gains haste [702.62a]. Casting it that way uses the alternative-cost rules [702.62d].

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes with more than two players. Sen Triplets targets one opponent, and only that opponent (the owner of the hand) can take the suspend special action; other players' hands are unaffected.

question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
Short answer: the provided context doesn't include the card text of Wayward Angel or Turn to Frog, so I can't state Wayward Angel's exact final power, toughness, colors, types, and abilities. What the rules I do have settle is the framework:

1. While manifested, Wayward Angel is a face-down permanent. A face-down permanent has no characteristics other than those listed by the ability or rules that let it be face down "manifest" makes it a 2/2 face-down creature with no name, no types, no abilities, and no mana cost, and those are its copiable values [708.2], [708.2a], [701.40h]. This is applied in layer 1b [613.2b].
2. When Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up, its copiable values revert to its normal printed values (its real name, mana cost, colors, types, printed power/toughness and abilities), but any effects that were already applied to it while it was face down continue to apply [708.8].
3. So Turn to Frog's continuous effect does not fall off when Wayward Angel is turned face up. Whatever type-changing/ability-removing part it has is applied in the later layers on top of the now face-up Wayward Angel, and any power/toughness-setting part is applied in layer 7 [613.1g]. In other words: start from Wayward Angel's real characteristics, then re-apply Turn to Frog's effect for its duration.
4. Note also that turning it face up is not an "enters the battlefield" event, so no enter-the-battlefield triggers of Wayward Angel occur [708.8]. And if Wayward Angel's printed power/toughness were defined by a "* " style ability keyed to cards in the graveyard, that would matter only if Turn to Frog doesn't remove abilities and doesn't set its power and toughness [208.2b].

To give the exact numbers I'd need Wayward Angel's printed text and Turn to Frog's printed text, plus whether Turn to Frog's effect is "until end of turn." This analysis is the same whether the table is two players or more.

question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
answer:
I can't fully resolve this with the material provided. The provided context includes no oracle text for Conspiracy, Kormus Bell, Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth, or Vastwood Zendikon, and it contains none of the layer rules (rule 613) that govern how type-changing and type-setting effects are ordered and applied. Those are exactly the pieces this question hinges on, so answering would require me to supply card text and layer rules from outside the context.

What the provided rules do establish, and which you'd need to combine with the missing card texts and layer rules:

- Creature types are subtypes shared by the creature and kindred card types, and Ferret is a legal creature type on the list [205.3m], [Creature Type], [302.3].
- A land can be a creature and a land at the same time; an effect that makes lands creatures gives the object both card types, and the object keeps its prior land types and supertypes [205.1b], [205.3c], [205.4b], [205.2b]. So a land named Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth being a creature while remaining a land is perfectly possible.
- Important distinction from [205.1b]: an effect that says something becomes an "artifact creature" leaves existing creature types alone, while an effect that says it becomes a "[creature type] artifact creature" replaces any existing creature types. An analogous distinction decides whether Vastwood Zendikon's type and Conspiracy's chosen Ferret type stack or overwrite each other — but I'd need the actual card texts and the layer/timestamp rules to say which wins.

If you paste the oracle text of Conspiracy, Kormus Bell, Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth, and Vastwood Zendikon plus rule 613 (layers) and 613.7 (dependency), I can give a definitive list of Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's creature types. Note also that everything above is about a single player's permanents, so nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

cited_text.302.3: Creature subtypes are usually a single word long and are listed after a long dash: “Creature — Human Soldier,” “Artifact Creature — Golem,” and so on. Creature subtypes are also called creature types. Creatures may have multiple subtypes. See rule 205.3m for the complete list of creature types. “Creature — Goblin Wizard” means the card is a creature with the subtypes Goblin and Wizard.
cited_text.205.1b: The type line is printed directly below the illustration. It contains the card’s card type(s). It also contains the card’s subtype(s) and supertype(s), if applicable. Some effects change an object’s card type, supertype, or subtype but specify that the object retains a prior card type, supertype, or subtype. In such cases, all the object’s prior card types, supertypes, and subtypes are retained. This rule applies to effects that use phrases such as “in addition to its other types” or that state that something is “still a [type, supertype, or subtype].” Some effects state that an object becomes an “artifact creature”; these effects also allow the object to retain all of its prior card types and subtypes. Some effects state that an object becomes a “[creature type or types] artifact creature”; these effects also allow the object to retain all of its prior card types and subtypes other than creature types, but replace any existing creature types. An ability reads, “All lands are 1/1 creatures that are still lands.” The affected lands now have two card types: creature and land. If there were any lands that were also artifacts before the ability’s effect applied to them, those lands would become “artifact land creatures,” not just “creatures,” or “land creatures.” The effect allows them to retain both the artifact and land card types. In addition, each land affected by the ability retains any land types and supertypes it had before the ability took effect. An ability reads, “All artifacts are 1/1 artifact creatures.” If a permanent is both an artifact and an enchantment, it will become an artifact enchantment creature.
cited_text.205.3c: Subtypes If a card with multiple card types has one or more subtypes, each subtype is correlated to its appropriate card type. Dryad Arbor’s type line says “Land Creature — Forest Dryad.” Forest is a land type, and Dryad is a creature type.
cited_text.205.4b: Supertypes An object’s supertype is independent of its card type and subtype, even though some supertypes are closely identified with specific card types. Changing an object’s card types or subtypes won’t change its supertypes. Changing an object’s supertypes won’t change its card types or subtypes. When an object gains or loses a supertype, it retains any other supertypes it had. An ability reads, “All lands are 1/1 creatures that are still lands.” If any of the affected lands were legendary, they are still legendary.
cited_text.205.2b: Card Types Some objects have more than one card type (for example, an artifact creature). Such objects satisfy the criteria for any effect that applies to any of their card types.
cited_text.Creature Type: Creature Type. A subtype that’s correlated to the creature card type and the kindred card type. See rule 302, “Creatures,” and rule 308, “Kindreds.” See rule 205.3m for the list of creature types.

answer_gold: It is an Elemental Ferret creature. Conspiracy has the earliest timestamp, but it's dependent on Vastwood Zendikon, and waits to apply until after Vastwood Zendikon is applied. Kormus Bell is dependent on Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth, so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is applied first, then Kormus Bell. At this point Conspiracy is no longer be dependent on Vastwood Zendikon, so Conspiracy is applied, and then Vastwood Zendikon.
